#9716. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

#9715. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

#9714. System One Models and the Future of AI Decision-Making

Models have been superhuman at chat for years, and the industry still can't point to where all the automation went.

Diogo Almeida, who helped build the instruction-following research that became ChatGPT, spent four years on that question before he left OpenAI. His answer, shipped in September 2026 as TypeSafe AI's Jev, is that the bottleneck was never raw intelligence. It's the interface. A model that replies in prose is an awkward component to build software on, because software doesn't consume sentences. It consumes values.

The class TypeSafe calls System One is named after the fast, intuitive thinking in Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow. A System One model takes unstructured state in and returns typed probabilistic decisions out, with no chat interface and no string generation. Using a general-purpose generative model in that role wastes tokens and processing time at scale.

Every pipeline I've built has the same point of friction: somewhere a language model writes prose and my code reads it back. The application wants a decision about keeping or deleting an email, or classifying a ticket as escalation. A frontier model generates a full paragraph containing the reasoning and the one-word decision, and the response gets routed through a parser to extract that word.

The waste shows up in four places at once. Output tokens cost three to eight times the input price on most providers, and a classification answer is mostly output. The response is a string, so it has to be parsed, and JSON mode wraps the real answer in a structure that can multiply the token count five to ten times on a small task like email classification. The value then needs validation against a schema, because a generative model can emit a response you never defined. And when any of that fails, retry blocks cost another full generation. A task whose substance is a single yes or no bills like a small essay.

There's a fifth cost that doesn't show on the invoice. A generative model is systematically overconfident. Ask for a confidence score and you get one, but the number isn't calibrated, so you can't branch on it. A model that's right 95% of the time and can't tell you which calls are in the other 5% can't run unattended. You keep a human in the loop because you have no way to know when the model needs one.

The agent loop makes this worse, because an agent makes a decision at every step. Every decision is another model call, and the loop slows down on retries and unverifiable responses.

Jev gives up string generation entirely. You declare the shape of the answer up front and call it like a function: send a state and a set of questions, and get the fields back filled in, each with a calibrated probability attached. TypeSafe describes it as a frontier-intelligence function call.

Parallel sampling. A chat model builds its answer one token at a time, each conditioned on the last. Jev fills every field in a single pass. TypeSafe reports end-to-end response times of 70 to 500 milliseconds against 3 to 329 seconds for frontier models, and you can ask several questions about the same state in one request without meaningfully changing the response time. That's where the 40x to 200x speed claims come from.

Schema conformance by construction. The possible outputs are enumerated before the call, so a wrong model decision cannot produce a type error. TypeSafe's 0% type-error figure is derived from the construction of the responses, not from testing.

Calibrated confidence. Every answer ships with a probability. TypeSafe trains with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD) instead of RLHF, so those probability numbers are genuinely accurate: if the confidence is high, the accuracy is high. That predictability is what makes the model composable into systems that run unattended.

The question types map onto what software actually asks. A Noul answers yes or no and returns the probability the statement is true. A Choice picks from a set of up to 255 options and returns a probability per option plus an overall confidence. A Score rates the input against ordered levels like low, medium, high. Keep or drop, route to tier two or tier three, is this urgent. Each question maps to a line of code that returns a typed value.

The pricing is the other half of the story. Jev costs $0.042 per million input tokens, and output is free, because there is no output in the billing sense. TypeSafe advertises it as 238 times cheaper on input than Claude Fable 5.1's $10 per million. A frontier chat model lists around $5 per million input and $25 to $30 per million output, and output is exactly where a classification answer lives.

Small numbers hide the story. Volume exposes it. Here's the cost function:

Run that at a million decisions a day and the difference stops being trivia. The generative model bills about $5,400 for that volume. Jev bills about $25. Third-party measurements land between the extremes: one group measured 1,000 eight-way routing decisions at $0.015 on Jev against $0.61 on GPT-5.6 Terra, about 40x. TypeSafe's own workflow evals claim 444.6x cheaper, and LangChain repeats 400x lower cost on classification tasks. Whatever the honest middle is, it's two orders of magnitude, and it's structural, not a price war.

The gap isn't because Jev is a smaller model that happens to be good enough. It's because a generative model bills you for the process of producing prose, and a decision doesn't need prose. Output tokens, parsing, validation, retries, and the uncertainty tax all disappear together because the model was built not to generate strings in the first place.

The instinct when you see that ratio is to reach for a cheaper generative model instead. That isn't the fix. A smaller generative model still produces a string, still needs parsing and validation, and still reports confidence you can't trust. It lowers the price per call and leaves the structural waste exactly where it was. The waste is in the interface, not the invoice.

Same routing decision, two implementations. First, the generative approach that most early pipelines used:

Now the System One version, using the TypeSafe SDK shape:

The second version has no parse step, no validation step, and no failure path where the model returns a value you didn't allow. The schema was part of the request, so the contract is enforced before the call rather than after it.

The difference that matters most is what happens with an ambiguous ticket. In the first version, confidence is a string the model made up. In the second, it's a number you can trust enough to branch on:

That branch is the whole automation argument in one line. When the model can tell you it's uncertain, you route the uncertain cases to a human and let the confident ones run unattended. The model doesn't need to be right every time. It needs to be honest about when it isn't, and the system around it becomes reliable even though the model isn't.

This isn't hypothetical for me. My own news filter uses a small Jev call to decide keep or drop before spending a full LLM on anything worth reading. A logged run came back at 354 input tokens and a probability, total. The expensive model never sees the boring stuff.

Nothing here argues against generative models. They're for open-ended reasoning and generation, and nothing replaces them there. The argument is about the division of labor inside an LLM operation: the big model thinks and writes, and the decision points around it run on something shaped like a function call.

The early deployments show the pattern. LangChain's Open SWE router originally classified requests with an LLM using structured output, then switched to Jev and made classification almost 50 times faster. In the A/B test that mattered, routing 973 agent threads across model tiers cut the median cost per thread 64%, from $2.61 to $0.94, with no measurable quality change. The same team ran the opposite experiment, routing everything to the cheapest model, and killed it within a day because engineers said output quality was disrupting their work. Cheapness was never the objective. Fitting the tool to the task was.

The guardrail pattern is the one I expect to spread. Coding harnesses like Claude Code and Cursor already classify dangerous actions before taking them, but the classifier lived in their closed-source code. A cheap, calibrated decision model lets any agent apply the same gate before a tool execution by asking Jev whether the call is risky, and blocking it if the answer is yes. LangChain shipped exactly that as Auto Mode middleware over Jev.

None of this requires believing TypeSafe's biggest numbers. The workflow-eval claims of 193.6x faster and 444.6x cheaper come from the vendor's own evaluations, built by its own team, scored against models the vendor chose. The intelligence-parity claim is only about System One shaped tasks, not general capability.

What you can verify yourself is the price, the latency on your own calls, and the schema guarantee, which is falsifiable by a single bad response. Treat the launch numbers as the ceiling, measure your own workload, and expect the real ratio to land somewhere between 40x and 400x. That's still a big number, and it doesn't depend on marketing.

The name Jev comes from William Stanley Jevons, the economist who noticed that making steam engines more efficient increased the demand for coal rather than reducing it. Cheaper steam meant more uses for steam. TypeSafe's bet is that machine intelligence follows the same path: every order of magnitude drop in the cost of intelligence unlocks orders of magnitude more use cases. Their own Doom demo runs about ten queries a second, which they estimate costs around seven dollars an hour, and their reaction was that this was cheaper than expected. A few years ago that sentence would not have existed.

The price and the interface put decisions inside ordinary code paths for the first time. The chatbot race never did that. When a routing decision costs a fraction of a cent and answers in a hundred milliseconds, you stop treating AI as a service you call for special occasions and start treating it as an if-statement that happens to be learned. Projects involving decision-making at scale, such as the map-reduce over a petabyte of unstructured data, or the email triage that never sleeps, never made sense at frontier prices with prose responses. They make sense at $0.042 per million input tokens with typed outputs.

Software was never waiting for a model that could write better. It was waiting for a model that could decide, cheaply enough and honestly enough to be trusted with the boring work. The big generative models will keep getting better at thinking and writing. The decisions in between will increasingly be made by models that don't write at all.

#9713. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#9712. I Watched AI Eat the Easy Half of an Industry. The Other Half Got More Expensive.

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

If you want to see what AI actually does to a professional services market, do not look at the think pieces. Look at logistics consulting. Over the past three years I have watched machine learning quietly absorb half of what this industry used to bill for, and the result is not what either the doomers or the boosters predicted. The analysts did not disappear. The market split, and the half that survived got more valuable.

A decade ago, a meaningful share of logistics consulting revenue came from work that was, honestly, computation: benchmark these freight rates, model this distribution network, forecast this demand curve, reconcile these invoices. It was skilled work, but it was pattern work, and pattern work is exactly what the current generation of models does at near-zero marginal cost.

Today a shipper with a data feed and a software subscription gets analysis that used to cost six figures. Arrival predictions come from models trained on historical movement data. Network scenarios run by the thousand. Document extraction reads the bills of lading that used to consume junior analysts. The report-writing tier of consulting, the firms whose deliverable was the analysis itself, is being hollowed out in real time, and nobody who buys consulting is mourning it.

The timeline matters for anyone mapping this onto their own industry. The hollowing did not announce itself. It showed up first as pricing pressure on commodity studies, then as procurement departments quietly canceling retainers for work their own tools now did, then as the mid-tier firms pivoting to implementation or disappearing into acquisitions. Three years, roughly, from capable models to restructured market. Professional services does not get a decade to adapt. It gets a product cycle.

A composite example, drawn from how these engagements actually run. An industrial shipper suspects it is overpaying for freight. Five years ago, step one was a six-week analytical phase billed by the hour. Today the benchmarking is largely done before the first meeting ends, because the consultant’s tooling has already scored every lane against live market data. What fills the engagement now is everything downstream of the analysis: deciding which carriers to pressure and which to protect, structuring a bid so incumbents actually compete, reading the counterparty across the table, sequencing the network changes so operations never hiccup.

Notice the economics. The part that was automated was the part that scaled with headcount, which is why junior analyst hiring in this field has cratered. The part that remains scales with reps, the hundreds of negotiations and implementations that calibrate someone’s judgment, and reps cannot be batch-processed. The pyramid business model died; the expertise business replaced it.

Here is the part the automation narrative misses. When the computable layer of a profession becomes free, the non-computable layer does not shrink. It becomes the entire product, and its price goes up, because buyers can finally see what they were actually paying for.

Economists have a name for the pattern: complementarity. Automate one input and its complements appreciate. Spreadsheets did not kill accounting; they killed ledger clerks and made judgment-heavy advisory the growth business. Databases did not kill law; they killed document review hours and raised the premium on courtroom strategy. The models are running the same play on analysis itself, across every industry at once, and freight just happens to be the cleanest place to watch it because the complement is so unmistakably physical.

In logistics, the non-computable layer is specific and stubborn. A model can tell you that you are overpaying on a freight lane. It cannot sit across the table from the carrier’s pricing manager, know from two hundred prior negotiations that the first offer is theater, and restructure the volume commitment so both sides sign. It can flag that your railcars dwell too long at a customer site. It cannot know that the fix runs through one specific unloading crew and a demurrage clause written in 2019. The deepest version of this is rail, the most contract-heavy and relationship-dense mode in freight, where specialist rail consulting practices staffed by former railroad executives are thriving in exactly the era that was supposed to automate them away.

Watch where the demand moved. Rankings of the best logistics consulting firms are now led by execution-focused specialists rather than report factories, and the fastest-growing firms in the field are boutiques built by operators, small teams of people who ran freight networks for decades, armed with the same AI tooling as everyone else, selling the one thing the tooling cannot produce: judgment with skin in the game. Many now tie fees directly to documented savings. You do not offer that pricing model unless you are confident you possess something the software does not.

The buyers repriced too, which is the half of the story nobody writes about. Procurement departments that once compared consultancies on day rates now compare them on referenceable outcomes, because the day-rate layer is software now. The RFP questions changed in three years from describe your methodology to show us the twelve-month results of your last three engagements. Markets learn fast when the alternative is free.

If you are building AI products for any operational industry, this split is your map. The computable layer is a feature war you will fight against every funded competitor, with margins trending toward zero. The durable business sits at the interface between the model output and the messy human system that has to act on it, and that interface is owned by whoever has the domain judgment.

Concretely, that suggests three build strategies that hold up. Sell to the experts rather than around them, because the operators-with-tooling model is winning and they are buying. Price against outcomes the way the leading consultancies now do, because outcome pricing is a moat software-only competitors cannot cross without the judgment layer. And if you must pick between a better model and better domain distribution, pick distribution, because the model advantage decays in months and the trust advantage compounds for years.

Which suggests the uncomfortable, useful conclusion: the most defensible asset in the AI era is not the model. It is the twenty years someone spent on loading docks and in negotiation rooms learning what the data cannot say. The software made that knowledge more valuable, not less, and the industries that figure out how to pair the two, as freight is doing right now, are the ones to watch.

Every knowledge industry is running this experiment with a lag. Freight just finished the first lap, and the results are posted: the analysts who were really computers lost, the operators who were really judges won, and the total value of the market went up. Plan your career, your product, and your hiring accordingly.

This story was distributed as a release by Jon Stojan under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging Program

#9711. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly:  When it comes to English grammar, there are two Big Players that everyone knows of: the Grammarly and ProWritingAid. but you are wondering which one to choose so here we write a detail article which will help you to choose the best one for you so Let's start

What is Grammarly?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.


Features of Grammarly

  • Spelling and Word Suggestion: Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a Personal Dictionary: The Grammarly app allows you to add words to your personal dictionary so that the same mistake isn't highlighted every time you run Grammarly.
  • Different English Style: Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Plagiarism: This feature helps you detect if a text has been plagiarized by comparing it with over eight billion web pages.
  • Wordiness: This tool will help you check your writing for long and hard-to-read sentences. It also shows you how to shorten sentences so that they are more concise.
  • Passive Voice: The program also notifies users when passive voice is used too frequently in a document.
  • Punctuations: This feature flags all incorrect and missing punctuation.
  • Repetition: The tool provides recommendations for replacing the repeated word.
  • Proposition: Grammarly identifies misplaced and confused prepositions.

  • Plugins: It offers Microsoft Word, Microsoft Outlook, and Google Chrome plugins.


What is ProWritingAid?

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing. 

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Features of ProWriting Aid

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

  • Grammar checker and spell checker: This tool helps you to find all grammatical and spelling errors.
  • Find repeated words:  The tool also allows you to search for repeated words and phrases in your content.
  • Context-sensitive style suggestions:  You can find the exact style of writing you intend and suggest if it flows well in your writing.
  • Check the readability of your content: Pro Writing Aid helps you identify the strengths and weaknesses of your article by pointing out difficult sentences and paragraphs.
  • Sentence Length: It also indicates the length of your sentences.
  • Check Grammatical error: It also checks your work for any grammatical errors or typos, as well.
  • Overused words: As a writer, you might find yourself using the same word repeatedly. ProWritingAid's overused words checker helps you avoid this lazy writing mistake.
  • Consistency: Check your work for inconsistent usage of open and closed quotation marks.
  • Echoes: Check your writing for uniformly repetitive words and phrases.

Difference between Grammarly and Pro-Writing Aid

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

Grammarly vs ProWritingAid

  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas the ProWritingAid interface is not friendly as Grammarly.

  • Grammarly does not offer much feedback on big picture writing; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.
  • Grammarly is a better option for accuracy, whereas ProWritingAid is better for handling fragmented sentences and dialogue. It can be quite useful for fiction writers.

#9710. Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

#9709. Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them

Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:

Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in three ways:

-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

#9707. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

#9706. Formbook Targets European Manufacturing and Technology Businesses with Localized Order Lures

Online interactive sandbox for DFIR/SOC investigations. Fast malware analysis and cybersecurity threat detection.

Online interactive sandbox for DFIR/SOC investigations. Fast malware analysis and cybersecurity threat detection.

Online interactive sandbox for DFIR/SOC investigations. Fast malware analysis and cybersecurity threat detection.

European businesses, particularly in the UK and Italy, face malware campaigns that exploit routine business correspondence. A recent Formbook (now also known as XLoader) campaign uses localized order and procurement lures to deliver an information stealer.

Manufacturing and technology companies are especially exposed because employees regularly handle purchase orders, supplier documents, and payment requests. A seemingly routine attachment can hide a JavaScript loader that ultimately deploys malware to steal browser-stored credentials.

The ANY.RUN team investigated the campaign, uncovering its infection chain, persistence methods, and links to other malware activity. These findings show how behavioral analysis and threat intelligence can help organizations strengthen their defenses.

The Formbook campaign relies on a familiar social engineering approach: making malicious attachments look like documents employees would normally receive as part of their work.

One of the analyzed archives, Nova narudžba 0148-712.zip, contains a JavaScript file with a Croatian/Bosnian title meaning “New Order”. Other related samples use themes involving price lists, procurement requests, quotations, and bank transfers.

These lures reflect everyday business processes:

The analyzed activity included submissions from the UK and Italy, alongside countries in the Balkans and South Caucasus. The language and themes of the lures indicate that attackers adapt their delivery materials to different markets rather than relying on a single generic document.

For EU-based organizations operating across multiple countries, this creates an additional detection challenge: security teams cannot assume that suspicious attachments will always use the company’s primary working language.

The consequences of a successful Formbook infection can extend beyond an individual workstation:

The combination of convincing business lures and credential-stealing capabilities makes the activity relevant to organizations that depend on continuous supplier and customer communication.

Reduce Tier 1 to Tier 2 escalations by 30% and keep complex investigations moving.

The analyzed sample was classified as malicious activity associated with Formbook/XLoader. XLoader is an evolution of Formbook, so both names are used when describing the malware.

You can follow the full Formbook attack chain in this ANY.RUN Sandbox analysis.

The archive was submitted to Interactive Sandbox multiple times starting October 7, 2026, and appeared as an email attachment on October 23. The investigation revealed a multi-stage infection chain involving obfuscated JavaScript, hidden PowerShell execution, encrypted payload delivery, and process injection.

The infection consists of four main stages.

The infection starts with Nova narudžba 0148-712.zip, which contains a JavaScript file with the same name.

Approximately 2 MB in size, the script is heavily obfuscated using obfuscator.io techniques. Most of its content consists of a Base64-encoded PowerShell payload, with additional string encryption and shuffled execution logic making static analysis more difficult.

The command includes: -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -NonInteractive -NoLogo

These parameters hide the PowerShell window and bypass the default execution policy. The dropper also uses WMI to monitor the process and terminate it if it runs for more than 50 seconds.

For defenders, the combination of wscript.exe, hidden PowerShell execution, and randomly named scripts in temporary directories is worth investigating.

The dropped script acts as an AES loader, identified by the header PowerShell Modular AES Pipeline Loader.

It stores three Base64-encoded resources: the payload, encryption key, and initialization vector. After sanitizing and decoding them, the script uses AES-256-CBC to decrypt the next stage and executes it in memory through PowerShell’s ScriptBlock::Create() functionality.

The loader then clears its resource map and invokes garbage collection, reducing the artifacts available for disk-based analysis.

However, the infection is not completely fileless: the original JavaScript and intermediate PowerShell script remain useful sources of forensic evidence.

The decrypted PowerShell stage contains two components: a .NET injector named GHOST.dll and the final Formbook payload.

Protected with ConfuserEx, the injector uses process hollowing to execute Formbook inside the legitimate Windows process aspnet_compiler.exe.

A watchdog called Operate-Beacon checks every five seconds whether the process is running. If it is not, the loader reloads GHOST.dll and attempts injection again. ANY.RUN analysts observed 15 instances of aspnet_compiler.exe during the sandbox session.

Formbook subsequently moves into rekeywiz.exe, a legitimate Windows EFS-related utility. From there, it launches Firefox and creates a randomly named file in %TEMP%, consistent with the collection of browser databases before reading them.

The final payload is designed to steal browser-stored credentials and communicate with its command-and-control infrastructure.

Because the malware uses legitimate Windows processes as containers, defenders should examine parent processes, command-line arguments, execution context, and memory behavior rather than relying on process names alone.

The loader establishes persistence through several startup mechanisms using the naming pattern SystemUpdate_ps_*. The investigation identified:

The shortcut uses the description System Update Service and launches PowerShell with hidden parameters. The machine-wide Run key attempt may fail without administrator privileges, but the other mechanisms can still maintain persistence.

Formbook also communicates with external C2 infrastructure over HTTP port 80. Analysts identified two domains involved in the observed activity:

The sandbox recorded a GET request associated with a Formbook C2 check-in, along with POST requests linked to data transmission.

Notably, the traffic used a User-Agent impersonating an Android 4.1.1 tablet despite originating from a Windows environment. This mismatch can help defenders identify suspicious outbound HTTP traffic in proxy logs.

The domain www[.]hlushkova[.]top also changed its resolved IP address during the observation period. Since one of its IP addresses is associated with shared hosting, domain-based detection is preferable to blocking the IP alone.

Help your SOC uncover up to 58% more threats, speed up investigations, and improve detection.

The investigation revealed several artifacts that security teams can use to identify this infection chain and potentially detect related malware.

wscript.exe → powershell.exe → aspnet_compiler.exe

Unexpected Formbook activity inside rekeywiz.exe

www[.]hlushkova[.]top, www[.]stanbicfinanceug[.]com

Android 4.1.1 User-Agent from Windows hosts

The most useful detection strategy is to correlate these indicators rather than rely on a single filename or process.

For example, a PowerShell process is not inherently malicious. However, a hidden PowerShell instance launched by wscript.exe, executing a randomly named script from C:\Temp\, followed by repeated launches of aspnet_compiler.exe, provides a much stronger reason to investigate.

The same applies to persistence. A shortcut named SystemUpdate_ps_* masquerading as a system update service is considerably more suspicious when combined with the associated PowerShell execution pattern.

Investigating a suspicious attachment is just the first step. Security teams also need to identify related infrastructure, loader components, and behaviors across other attacks.

Interactive Sandbox lets SOC and MSSP analysts execute suspicious files and observe their behavior in real time, including process activity, command-line arguments, file and registry changes, and network connections, providing insights that static analysis may miss.

A powerful new feature inside ANY.RUN’s sandbox — Related Threat Context (Related analyses) — connects with Threat Intelligence Lookup and helps SOCs and MSSPs explore connected activity beyond the original sample.

ANY.RUN‘s global community of over 700,000 security professionals and 16,000 organizations contributes to a rich source of real-world threat data, helping analysts identify connections faster.

In this investigation, another malicious archive themed around business documentation used a similar JavaScript lure, providing an additional lead for examining recurring delivery techniques.

TI Lookup extends this investigation by searching sandbox data for specific indicators, artifacts, and behaviors. Several queries revealed how widely the observed techniques appeared in other malware activity.

The query filePath:”C:\\Temp\\ps_*.ps1″ returned 78 sandbox analyses from the previous 90 days. Besides Formbook, results included AgentTesla, DarkCloud, Remcos, XWorm, and Snake.

This suggests the temporary-script pattern can help investigate multiple information stealers and remote-access threats.

The query filePath:”*\\Startup\\SystemUpdate_ps_*.lnk” identified 42 analyses over 90 days. A search for the registry value SystemUpdate_ps_* returned 24.

These artifacts also appeared in activity involving AgentTesla, Remcos, XWorm, DarkCloud, AsyncRAT, and Snake Keylogger, suggesting a potentially shared loader or distribution mechanism.

Searching for the SHA-256 hash of GHOST.dll revealed that the same injector had appeared under the filename cloked_data.exe in a separate analysis on October 9, 2026.

This suggests the component may be reused across different builds, making it a useful lead when investigating activity beyond the original Formbook sample.

Searching for www[.]hlushkova[.]top returned 14 analyses dating back to August 2026.

The second domain, www[.]stanbicfinanceug[.]com, appeared in 7 analyses, with substantial overlap.

The associated attachments used different localized business themes, including:

For SOC and MSSP teams, this broader context turns one suspicious attachment into a starting point for discovering related samples, infrastructure, reusable loaders, and additional indicators.

Related Threat Context reduces repetitive IOC research for Tier 1 analysts and gives Tier 2 teams richer context for deeper investigations. By connecting alerts with existing threat intelligence, it helps security teams accelerate triage, reduce manual work, and make better-informed response decisions.

Give your SOC the context to cut manual research and achieve up to 94% faster triage.

Sandbox analysis and TI Lookup help analysts investigate incidents and uncover related threats. ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence Feeds extend this visibility by bringing validated IOCs and behavior-based intelligence into existing security systems.

ANY.RUN’s analysis found that up to 30% of unique malicious IOCs in Interactive Sandbox sessions had already been identified by ANY.RUN and were available in TI Feeds.

This means SOC and MSSP teams can match known indicators against their telemetry before manually investigating suspicious files in the Sandbox. For example, an integrated security solution can flag connections to known malicious infrastructure during routine monitoring.

The 30% finding highlights how existing intelligence can help detect threats before manual sandbox analysis is needed.

Some malware uses geographic checks, localized infrastructure, or environment-dependent logic, so its behavior may vary depending on the simulated victim’s location and locale.

ANY.RUN Interactive Sandbox supports residential proxies and locale settings, allowing analysts to reproduce regional environments. For example, when investigating threats targeting UK or Italian businesses, they can select a proxy and locale matching the target region to better observe geographically dependent behavior.

Presets make this workflow easier. Teams can save proxy and locale combinations for different regions and reuse them across investigations, avoiding repetitive setup and keeping analysis environments consistent.

The Formbook investigation shows how an ordinary business attachment can trigger a multi-stage infection designed to evade detection and steal corporate credentials.

For manufacturing and technology businesses across Europe, procurement documents, supplier requests, quotations, and payment correspondence provide convincing themes for social engineering.

Effective protection requires more than identifying suspicious files. Security teams must analyze malware behavior, investigate related threats, and apply intelligence to ongoing detection.

As a result, SOCs and MSSPs are able to accelerate investigations, improve detection coverage, and reduce the risk of corporate account and data compromise.

ANY.RUN helps SOC and MSSP teams investigate cyber threats, improve detection, and respond to incidents more efficiently. Its solutions give security professionals the tools and intelligence they need to understand attacks and make informed decisions.

The ANY.RUN solutions include Interactive Sandbox for analyzing suspicious files, URLs, and phishing activity with Threat Intelligence capabilities, such as Threat Intelligence Lookup, Threat Intelligence Feeds, and Threat Intelligence Reports. These capabilities help teams connect related incidents, monitor changes in threat infrastructure, and use findings from real-world investigations to inform their security operations.

More than 16,000 organizations and 700,000 cybersecurity professionals worldwide rely on ANY.RUN. The company is SOC 2 Type II certified, demonstrating its commitment to protecting customer data through established security controls.
