#9705. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9704. Retrieval Ran First. Was Its Result Actually Ready?

The trace starts with retrieval. Generation appears underneath it. The ordering test passes.

But generation began while retrieval was still running.

“A appears before B” can describe the order in which events were encountered. “A's result was available before B began” describes an execution dependency. “B actually consumed A's result” is a stronger data-flow claim. They are not three ways of saying the same thing.

I maintain AgentInspect. This article tests those distinctions with controlled promises and agent-inspect@6.31.35. The fixture does not invoke a model, search engine, or vector database.

Avoid a demonstration that depends on a slow network. Hold retrieval open until the test explicitly releases it:

Here type: "llm" labels an instrumented boundary. It does not turn the callback into a model call or capture hidden reasoning. The callback returns a fixed string.

Retrieval is invoked before generation, but the result cannot become available until after generation completes. The fixture encodes that relationship without guessing a millisecond delay.

Start order is insufficient when the second operation depends on the first result.

After opening the generated file with openTraceFile from agent-inspect/readers, evaluate the relation:

Use the typed relation because this crosses a TOOL-to-LLM boundary. tools.requiredOrder is a tool-only surface, not a generic list of arbitrary workflow nodes.

TraceContract is beta, and steps.orderRelations is explicitly experimental in this release. Keep the version pin and test the exact semantics you intend to rely on.

The measured results for the overlap fixture are:

Overlap can produce diagnostic information even when first-occurrence ordering passes. Read findings and warnings, not only the top-level label.

all-occurrences is a global boundary, not an automatic pairing algorithm.

Consider a legitimate two-turn interaction: retrieve, generate, retrieve again, generate again. A rule requiring all retrieval to precede all generation can reject that workflow even if each individual answer waited for its own retrieval.

That is not a reason to weaken the rule until it passes. It is a reason to model the intended scope. Use separate runs or explicit application-level links that associate each answer with its retrieval result. Don’t assume that matching names imply pairwise dependency.

Similarly, requireEndpoints: true matters. An ordering statement should not quietly satisfy your product requirement when one of the necessary endpoints is missing.

The corresponding positive control awaits retrieval before invoking generation:

Inside a captured run, this fixture passes the tested all-occurrences relation. The change is the dependency in the application, not a delay inserted into the test.

For a real model call, completion still does not establish consumption. Record a bounded result reference at retrieval and the reference actually supplied to generation. An application assertion can compare those references without storing the retrieved document or prompt.

Even matching references prove wiring, not factual grounding. Whether the answer uses the evidence correctly requires a separate domain or semantic check.

The current implementation has a narrower boundary worth documenting. In the companion fixture, one generate_answer starts early and never finishes; another matching generation completes later. The isolated all-occurrences ordering rule passes, while the full contract with completion checking fails through run.status.

This was reproduced against 6.31.35. It is not a claim that the ordering rule completely diagnoses every unfinished occurrence. Do not ship an ordering-only gate or describe that diagnostic gap as fixed.

The test deliberately creates an unawaited pending operation to expose the boundary. That is a negative control, not an application pattern to copy. Keep a valid fixture, an overlap fixture, a repeated-turn fixture, and an incomplete fixture in your contract tests.

A trace can establish that a recorded step preceded another. With adequate timestamps and boundaries, it can establish that one finished before the other began. With application-owned references, it can help establish which result was supplied downstream.

None of those facts alone proves that an answer is correct.

The practical improvement is to name the obligation precisely. If generation needs retrieval output, test result availability. If it must use a particular retrieval result, test the data-flow link. If the answer must be grounded, test the answer against that evidence.

One green ordering check should not have to impersonate all three.

Across high-volume SaaS, FinTech, and telemetry platforms operating in US-East, London, and Frankfurt regions, monolithic PostgreSQL tables crossing 500 million rows silently degrade p99 read latencies and trigger catastrophic autovacuum wraparound stalls.

Traditional schema migrations force maintenance windows that violate strict enterprise SLAs, leaving backend teams trapped between bloated B-tree indexes and risky table locks.

Why Monolithic Indexes Collapse Under Multi-Region Write Bursts When append-heavy event tables grow beyond shared buffer memory, every single INSERT forces random page reads across deep B-tree levels. Even on high-IOPS NVMe storage in AWS us-east-1 or GCP europe-west1, cache hit ratios plummet below 82%, causing I/O wait spikes and connection pool exhaustion inside PgBouncer.

Shadow Table Cutover & Declarative Partition Pruning Instead of running blocking ALTER TABLE locks, senior infrastructure teams deploy a dual-write trigger bridge into a declaratively partitioned shadow table—allowing PostgreSQL 17's query planner to prune 98% of cold partitions at execution time.

By combining declarative range and hash sub-partitioning with pre-warmed monthly partition attachments, teams eliminate AccessExclusiveLock bottlenecks during live production cutovers.

Non-Blocking Constraint Validation: Add CHECK constraints using NOT VALID first, then validate constraints in a separate transaction to avoid locking live traffic.

Automated Cold Tier Archival: Detach partitions older than 90 days concurrently and stream Parquet snapshots directly to object storage without triggering autovacuum storms.

#9700. What is piloncillo? This sweetener makes great cookies, pan dulce, and more: Use this traditional Mexican unrefined sugar for a dash of flavor and history.

This article is part of our feature celebrating Pan Dulce. Find all things pan dulce here.

Categorically, piloncillo is a “non-centrifugal” cane sugar, meaning it is an unrefined sugar product and a true natural brown sugar. It’s mostly consumed in Mexico and Latin America, but a similar product can be found in Asia, known as jaggery in India. Though often lumped together, these unrefined dark sugars are very different from brown sugars on the market today, which have been refined to a large degree — in some cases, they’re actually just white sugar with coloring or molasses added.

Making piloncillo, on the other hand, involves an artisanal process that’s hundreds of years old. To make it, pressed cane juice is boiled to evaporate the water and deeply caramelize the sugar. The cooked cane is then poured into molds (often made of wood) and left to dry and harden. Traditional piloncillo is conical in shape and can vary in size from small to large cones but is most commonly found in a medium size that weighs about 200 grams. In Guatemala and Colombia, it is called panela, where it is cooked to a lighter degree and typically formed into a brick, rather than cone, shape. Other forms of piloncillo can be granulated or liquid (which is more rare).

Minimally processed and boldly flavored, piloncillo was historically a prized and respected foodstuff. As an unrefined cane sugar, piloncillo provides more complex vitamins and minerals than refined sugars, which undergo processing and whitening methods that also strip nutrients from the whole food. And piloncillo is also great for baking, providing notes of burnt caramel and hints of smoke. Plus, its rich molasses qualities keep baked goods moist and fresh for longer.

Always look at the ingredient label when purchasing piloncillo and make sure it says 100% pure cane juice or cane sugar. It is becoming increasingly common to find imitation products marketed as jaggery or piloncillo that contain coloring and corn syrup. You can find good piloncillo at specialty grocery stores or online at retailers.

In Mexico and throughout Latin America, piloncillo is an important ingredient in many traditional dishes. (Some will even say it’s not the “real dish” if you substitute sugar in these recipes due to the deep flavors and richness that only piloncillo can provide.) This deep, dark unrefined sugar lends its characteristic flavor and texture to popular foods and beverages such as capirotada, tepache, coyotas, atole, café de olla, calabaza al horno, coricos, and hojarascas, to name a few!

I love adding piloncillo when I’m making champurrado. In this warm and thick chocolate beverage, the piloncillo is chopped or grated and dissolved in the pot with water or milk before adding the chocolate and masa. In this recipe, the piloncillo’s intense sweet and smoky flavors pair well with the chocolate and corn masa.

While there are many dishes and uses for piloncillo, it’s not a simple substitution for granulated white sugar in recipes, but you can use it the same as you would brown sugar with a 1:1 substitution by weight.  Depending on how hard the cone is, it can be crumbled or grated for easier measuring. If it is very hard, try cutting it in half with a sharp knife and then placing it between parchment paper or a towel and beating with a rolling pin.

#9699. Could AI Agents Unlock Crypto Mass Adoption?

Crypto geek and founder of ARPA Network and Bella Protocol.

Crypto geek and founder of ARPA Network and Bella Protocol.

Crypto geek and founder of ARPA Network and Bella Protocol.

Crypto’s promise of mass adoption has echoed for more than a decade but despite 2026 now coming to a close, it is clear that the wait is still on. To this point, even though about 30% of American adults own some form of crypto, the numbers are still at the same level they were back in 2023.

Now, if one were to compare these same figures with AI, the trend seems quite clear, i.e., ChatGPT alone reached 900 million weekly users by Q1 of this year (with over five percent of these individuals being paying customers). Similarly, Stanford's latest AI Index has revealed that generative AI is already seeing mass adoption levels within just three years of the tech going mainstream.

Put simply, while one technology (i.e. crypto) is riddled with complexities such as seed phrases, gas fees, and network selection, the other just asks users to type in a question.

From the outside looking in, price swings still top the list of worries when it comes to crypto followed by a long list of usability complaints, such as:

These worries are not irrational. In its 2025 Internet Crime Report, released this April, the FBI recorded approximately $11.4 billion in reported losses involving cryptocurrency, with people aged 60 and over accounting for roughly $4.4 billion.

AI could help reduce some of the operational complexity users face. Coinbase’s Agentic Wallets, for instance, isolate private keys from the AI agent and provide programmable spending limits. The product is aimed at developers, but the design points toward a broader possibility.

Keeping private keys out of an agent’s reach is an important safeguard, but it does not guarantee that every transaction it requests is appropriate. Spending limits need to be enforced outside the model, permissions should be easy to revoke, and users need a clear record of what they authorized and what was executed. As the interface becomes simpler, those controls become more important.

Picture someone asking a chatbot to send $50 to a relative abroad. A well-designed system could identify a supported payment route, calculate the total fee and show what the recipient would receive before asking for confirmation. Stablecoins could provide the settlement layer where they offer an advantage in cost, speed or availability.

Users would not need to select the network manually, but they would still need to understand and approve the payment. The recipient would also need a practical way to use or withdraw the funds.

The crypto side of the transaction could become largely unseen infrastructure. The meaningful financial decisions would remain visible.

The infrastructure for this shift is already taking shape. Coinbase’s x402 payment protocol, launched in May 2025, enables stablecoin payments over HTTP, allowing applications and agents to pay for resources such as APIs and digital services.

This extends the opportunity beyond consumer payments. An assistant completing a task could purchase access to the information or computing resources it needs, within a budget set by its user.

Still, transaction counts alone cannot establish how much useful commerce is taking place. The more meaningful questions concern what is being purchased, whether the service is delivered and whether people return because the experience works.

Security requires similar care in interpreting the numbers. The FBI’s recent report included its first dedicated section on AI, recording 22,364 AI-related complaints and nearly $893 million in reported losses. These figures cover AI-related crime broadly, including impersonation and scams, rather than losses specifically caused by agentic wallets.

For AI systems handling payments, the implications are clear: hard spending limits, understandable confirmations and clear responsibility when something goes wrong. A record showing that money moved is only part of the picture. Users also need to know whether the action matched their instructions.

The next wave of adoption may come from people who want a simpler way to complete a task, whether that means sending money or paying for a digital service. AI assistants could give them a familiar interface, with crypto providing the underlying infrastructure where it offers a practical advantage.

The opportunity is to make those services useful without requiring people to become crypto experts first.

None of this can happen on its own. If AI makes crypto easier to use without making it safer, it risks making scams and mistakes more efficient. But if the guardrails hold up, the next jump in adoption may look less like a rush to sign up for exchanges and more like people moving money through AI assistants, with crypto running quietly underneath.

AI Is Making Critical Decisions. Verifiable Machine Learning Makes Them Accountable.

#9698. 8 Pantry Items Pro Organizers Say You Should Toss ASAP

Your expired spices and stale snacks are taking up prime shelf space.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

No one wants to waste perfectly good food—I’m more likely to eat something slightly past its expiration date than throw it out prematurely—but some pantry items are just taking up space.

Dusty canned foods, old spices, expired baking ingredients, and more past-their-prime goods serve little to no culinary value. Getting rid of them will actually help you identify the pantry items that you can still use before they go bad. But how can you keep your pantry organized more regularly, and what exactly should you throw away?

Go through every item in your pantry at least twice a year, recommends Nicole Gabai, professional organizer, founder of B. Organized, and author of The Art of Organizing: An Artful Guide to an Organized Life.

If a twice-yearly check-in feels too daunting, consider a weekly five-minute check-in to discard expired goods, says Shaniece Jones, professional organizer and founder of Closet Therapy. “Organize by accessibility and intention,” she says. “Keep your daily go-tos at eye level, heavy items like large cans of oil and bottled water on lower shelves, and seasonal or rarely used items up high.” Labels, Lazy Susans, and drawer dividers are some of her go-to tools for organizing the pantry.

As you start cleaning, check off the following items—these are some of the most common pantry items our organizing experts find past their prime.

While many shelf-stable foods, such as canned goods, are still safe to eat past their expiration date, you should still check for signs of spoilage. “You can tell canned goods have spoiled if they are rusted, or if you see the cans bulge or dent,” Gabai says.

Labeling pantry items helps you check how long they’ve been open. For opened packages and bulk goods you’ve decanted into containers, write the date on the label so you know when you opened them.

Spices that have lost their smell? Time to go. “If it smells flat or just not aromatic, then it needs to be replaced since it will add very little, if any, flavor to what you’re cooking,” Gabai says. She also notes that ground spices typically last one to two years, while dried herbs can last up to three years.

“Baking ingredients like flour, baking powder, and baking soda can lose their effectiveness over time,” says Meaghan Kessman, founder of Meaghan Kessman Home Organization.

Eventually, flour will go bad, but how long it takes to get rancid depends on how it’s stored and the type of flour. In general, Gabai says it will last at room temperature for six to eight months. She recommends storing it in an airtight container in the fridge or freezer.

“Check for expiration dates and any signs of spoilage, such as clumping or an off smell,” Kessman says. “If you’re unsure, test baking powder by adding a teaspoon to hot water—if it bubbles, it’s still good to use.”

We often buy cooking oils in bulk, but keep in mind that they eventually go bad. “Oils and fats, such as olive oil, vegetable oil, and shortening, can become rancid if stored for too long. Rancid oils have a sour or off smell,” Kessman says. “Always check the expiration date and store oils in a cool, dark place to keep them fresh longer.”

Gabai recommends storing oils in a cool, dark place and disposing of them properly; freeze in a zip-top bag, then toss in the trash (never pour down the drain).

These pantry staples are oil-rich, so they spoil faster than you might think. “They can last about 6 months at room temperature, but if you freeze them, they can last a year or more,” Gabai says.

“Snacks and cereals can go stale quickly once opened,” Kessman says. She recommends checking expiration dates and signs of staleness, like an unusual smell or texture.

According to Gabai, grains, rice, and beans can last about one to two years, but brown rice and other whole grains will not last as long because of their higher oil content.

“Condiments like ketchup, mustard, and salad dressings often get pushed to the back of the pantry and forgotten,” Kessman says. “Check for expiration dates and any signs of separation, discoloration, or off smells.”

Honey is the rare exception that probably isn't spoiled. The National Honey Board states that honey has a shelf life of approximately two years, although it can last much longer if stored correctly in a sealed container.

“Honey was found in the tombs of kings and royalty as far back as 3,000 years in Egypt—and it was still edible!” Gabai notes.

If you notice crystallization, Gabai recommends gently heating the honey container in a pot of water.

#9697. The Most-Broken Package on Our New Site Never Actually Broke

We just put a page on the web for every package we have read breaking changes for: 2,495 of them this morning, on npm, PyPI, crates.io and eleven other registries. Each one lists what a release removed, renamed or changed, with its source.

The package at the very top, with more breaking changes than anything else on the list, is happy-dom. 13,444 of them in 30 versions.

It did not break 13,444 times. Almost none of that is real. This is the story of the fake number, the cleanup we wrote to remove it, and the dry run that showed the cleanup wanted to rewrite 31,368 rows that were perfectly fine.

On Nov 17, while we were getting the package pages ready, happy-dom stood out by a mile. Every patch release "removed" hundreds of members, 429 of them with names like this:

That is TypeScript's internal name for a member keyed by a symbol, and the number at the end is the symbol's id in one particular compile. Build the same code again and the number changes. So every release looked like it had deleted a pile of members and added a pile of identical ones with new numbers. Nothing had changed. The names were just not stable from one build to the next.

The fix going forward was easy: name such a member the way a person writes it, [window] or [Symbol.iterator], so two builds of the same code agree.

That left the rows already stored. Production held 19,784 of them across 52 packages on Nov 17. They had leaked into answers and fix inputs, and pushed packages up the rankings. If you open happy-dom's page this morning (Nov 18), it still says 13,444. That number is the bug. They had to go.

We already had a backfill job, a script that walks stored releases and brings their rows up to date with today's rules. Adding one rule to it was the obvious move: a row keyed by a name with a compile-time symbol id is withdrawn as "no longer found".

We ran it on production with writes turned off first. Not out of wisdom. It is just how that script runs unless you tell it otherwise.

The first number made sense. It had grown a little since the day before, to 19,829 across 53 packages. The second number made no sense at all. The rule we had added does not touch titles.

The obvious explanation was that the titles really were stale. The backfill rebuilds a row's title with today's titling code, and if titles had been written by older code, a rebuild would update them. Thirty thousand old titles getting a refresh sounded almost plausible.

So we checked when the rows were written.

Every live row of that kind in production, 559,035 of them, was written after Oct 29. The code that writes titles had not changed since Oct 28. Every one of those titles was written by the exact code the backfill was about to use to "fix" them.

There was no such thing as an old title in that table. Whatever the backfill was doing, it was not catching up. It was drifting.

When the reading of a release finds two changes that are really one (say, two members deprecated together), it folds them into one row with a title that names both:

The row keeps the list of members it covers, but in a separate field from the one the backfill read when it rebuilt titles. So the rebuild saw one member, wrote a title naming one member, and called that an update. Rebuilt from the stored row, that title lost its second half.

The title was right. The rebuild was the thing that was wrong, because it was rebuilding from less than the original writer had.

The other kind was quieter. When a release is first read, the package is named the way its registry spells it: NumSharp. The backfill named it by an internal key that is lowercased for matching: numsharp.

Same package, a different string. Every title that contained the name differed by case, so every one of them looked "changed" and went on the rewrite list.

Neither of these is a dramatic bug. Both are the same mistake: a correction job recomputed a value from what it had, instead of from what the original writer had, and treated every difference as a fix.

The rule we landed on: a title stands as the reading wrote it, unless this run changes what the row names. If the run folds a copy into a row, or drops a claim so the row now says something different, the title is rebuilt. Otherwise the title is not the backfill's business.

The package name now comes from the registry's own spelling, the same place the original reading got it.

While we were in there, a second read-through found one more disagreement. The backfill marked a rule as stale for a copy of a member under another entry point of the same package, because its name split ignored a single :. The code that stores new changes already split it correctly. Two places answering the same question in two ways is a bug by itself, so both now call one function.

Then we ran the read-only pass again over all 14,631 production release steps:

The withdrawals did not move. The 31,368 went to zero. The 20 folds are real duplicates, like a rename stored once from the release notes and once from a diff of the code, which should always have been one row.

Honestly, nothing clever. The script defaults to a dry run, and the dry run reports each kind of change as its own count, not one total. If it had printed "51,197 rows updated", it would have been easy to shrug. Two separate lines, one of them for a kind of change nobody asked for, are hard to shrug at.

And the question that cracked it was not "is the new rule right?". The new rule was fine. It was "when were these rows written, and by what code?". Once the answer was "by today's code, all of them", there was nothing left for a title rewrite to correct, so every rewrite had to be a bug.

A correction job carries two kinds of risk. There is the rule you meant to add, which you test. And there is everything else the job does on every run, which nobody looks at any more because it has always been a no-op. The second kind is the one that rewrites 31,000 good rows.

Before a stored-data correction writes anything, ask when the rows were written. A rule meant for rows older than the fix may match nothing, and then it rewrites what is right.

And if you want to see what the packages you use really broke, the pages are at since.dev/packages. Take happy-dom's number with a grain of salt until the cleanup lands.

What's the closest a migration or backfill of yours came to rewriting data that was already correct?

I'm Nabil. I build Since, which tracks what your code depends on and tells you before it breaks.

#9696. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9695. Nara Smith’s Mom’s Pasta

In our Cooking With Friends series, friends of Delish visit the Test Kitchen to share their favorite recipes with you. Happy cooking!

This is my mom’s recipe, and it taught me what simple abundance really looks like. She’d grate tomatoes and spoon the sauce over her native South African pap (a dish made from cornmeal, similar to grits or polenta), rice, ground beef, or almost anything that needed a little love. I couldn’t believe something so good could come from a handful of ingredients, and she showed me that with this dish it’s not about adding more, but how you handle what you have.

The magic is in the grating. It separates the sweet tomato pulp and leaves the skins behind, giving you the pure heart of the fruit. Please don’t skip the beef bouillon—it gives the sauce its deeper savory backbone. I love this tossed with freshly made spaghetti or tagliatelle, though dried pasta works beautifully, too—exactly like my mom makes it. You can enjoy this year-round, but it’s especially delightful in summer, when tomatoes taste like the sun.

#9694. The Air Says +5 C. The Road Says -1. Surface Temperature From 3,501 Stations in 10 Countries.

Posted on Nov 18 • Originally published at napspan.com

A weather forecast gives you the temperature of the air, about two metres above the ground. A truck drives on the road. On a clear autumn night the two can be several degrees apart, and the road is the colder one: asphalt radiates its heat to the sky, a bridge deck loses it from both sides, and the first ice of the season forms on a surface that is below zero under air that is not.

Road authorities measure the road itself. Their roadside weather stations carry a sensor in the asphalt, and most of them publish what it reads. We carry 4,195 road-weather stations across 10 European countries, and 3,501 of them publish a road-surface temperature — now under one field name, surface_temperature_c, whichever country the station stands in.

Updated 18 November 2026: the coverage figures and the table below were re-measured, and Finland (532 stations, added on 16 November) is now in the set. The readings from 9 October are kept as the moment they describe.

At 07:00 UTC on 9 October 2026, 191 stations reported a road surface at or below 0 °C. At 31 of them the air was above freezing, and at 7 it was above +2 °C. Across all 2,721 stations that publish both readings, the road was colder than the air at 737 — more than one in four.

A route plan built on air temperature sees nothing at either place. That is the case this data exists for.

The E6 crosses from Sweden into Norway at Svinesund. Ask for every road-weather station within 25 km of the bridge:

On the morning of 9 October that returned nine stations — four Swedish, five Norwegian — in one list. One from each side, trimmed:

On the bridge itself the road was 3.2 degrees colder than the air. Thirteen kilometres north on the E6 it was 0.2 degrees colder. Same morning, same corridor — which is why one temperature per route is not enough.

The Norwegian row above carries the surface temperature twice. That is deliberate, and it is the reason this post exists.

Until 8 October, road-surface temperature reached our API under five different keys, one per national convention: surface_temperature_c from Germany, Sweden and Poland, road_surface_temperature_c from Norway and Iceland, road_temperature_c from Lithuania, surface_temp_c from Scotland, and road_surface_temp_c from Slovenia and Latvia — Latvia’s one level down, inside a nested object. Air temperature, dew point, humidity and wind direction were split the same way. A client reading surface_temperature_c saw the road in three countries and nothing in six, and nothing errored.

Since 8 October every station also carries the common key. The original key stays, because someone may already be reading it; the common one is added next to it. Where a country already used the common name, nothing changed. Finland, added on 16 November, arrived under it.

Measured in one transaction against production on 18 November 2026, 07:11 UTC:

Some stations measure only air or wind and have no surface sensor at all. Scotland is the only part of the United Kingdom in the set, and Poland is five stations, not a national network.

While pulling the figures for this post, fifteen Swedish stations reported a road surface of exactly 0.0 °C under air as warm as +10.7 °C. They were not icy. The national feed sends a sensor that has no reading as an empty record, and our parser turned “no reading” into zero — the same mistake gave 50 Swedish stations a visibility of 0 m. Fixed on 9 October: a sensor that sends no value now produces no field. Every Swedish figure on this page was measured after the fix.

Surface condition is in the agency’s own words. 2,139 stations in six countries describe the road surface — dry, wet, glaze from Germany, Wet and Moist from Scotland, Wet and salty from Finland, Šlapia (“wet”) from Lithuania. We carry the word as published under surface_condition and do not map it onto a shared scale: the scales do not line up, and a translated “wet” that the agency meant as “wet and treated” is worse than the original. Sweden publishes ice, water and snow flags for a few dozen of its stations (56 of 837 on 9 October); we do not carry those yet.

Some sensors publish impossible numbers, and we pass them through. On 9 October, 26 stations published a pair of readings that cannot both be true (on 18 November, 16) — a road surface of −75 °C on the A45 in Germany under +5.8 °C air, or air of −40 °C on the E6 in northern Norway over a +1.3 °C road. The 9 October figures in this post leave those 26 out. The API does not: it returns what the road authority published, and a sanity check against the air temperature belongs in your code.

Not every country says when the reading was taken. Germany, Sweden, Finland and Latvia stamp each observation with observation_time, Poland with measure_time. Norway, Iceland, Lithuania, Scotland and Slovenia do not. Where the stamp exists, check it: on 9 October, the oldest Swedish observation still being published was five days old.

Units are in the field name. _c is Celsius, _ms metres per second, _pct percent, _m metres. Where a feed does not state its unit we do not guess one: Scotland’s wind speed is carried as published and has no wind_speed_ms.

It is a measurement, not a forecast. Each reading is what the sensor saw when it last reported. Nothing here predicts where ice will form in two hours.

Road-weather stations are one more feature type in the same /features schema as road cameras, live truck-parking occupancy and truck restrictions and VMS messages. A camera shows a person the road; a surface sensor gives your code a number. Filter by jurisdiction with ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 codes (NOR, SWE), by bbox, or by a point and radius_km as above.

Coverage figures and the table measured against production on 18 November 2026, 07:11 UTC, in a single transaction. The frost readings, the Svinesund example, the impossible-pair count and the observation ages are from 9 October 2026, 07:00 UTC. Readings change by the minute, and a winter morning will look nothing like this October one — the coverage and the field names are what will hold.

#9693. The Technical Challenges of Moving Tokenized Deposits Between Banks

Tech Writer | AI, Cybersecurity & Software Content Specialist

Tech Writer | AI, Cybersecurity & Software Content Specialist

Tech Writer | AI, Cybersecurity & Software Content Specialist

A bank can issue a deposit token on a blockchain and let approved customers transfer it around the clock. But when the recipient uses a different bank, spending that money may require extra steps.

Suppose a company receives $500,000 in tokenized deposits from a trading partner. The tokens arrive in its wallet, and the company wants to use the funds to pay a supplier through its usual bank. If that bank cannot accept the tokens, the company must find another way to access the money, such as redeeming the tokens with the issuing bank and transferring the funds through an existing payment system.

For a business managing money across several banks, that extra step can limit the usefulness of tokenized deposits. The transfer may be quick, but the recipient still needs a practical way to use the funds.

Banks are working on this problem as they bring deposits onto programmable networks. Improving blockchain performance helps, but it does not settle the questions that arise when money moves between institutions.

A tokenized deposit represents a deposit held in a commercial bank. It means that the deposit stays with the bank regardless of where the transactions related to it are executed on the blockchain.

A token issued by Bank A is not necessarily a deposit with Bank B just because it is delivered to Bank B's customer. The recipient bank must understand whether it can accept the token, what rights the holder has and how to process the payment.

Let us go back to the firm that receives the $500,000. Its treasury staff can cash out the tokens from Bank A and transfer the funds through a traditional payment method. Alternatively, the two banks can come to an agreement that would enable them to clear the transaction without requiring the recipient to handle the original tokens.

Both approaches depend on rules that the institutions recognize and are prepared to follow. Bank B needs to know when it can credit the company's account and what to do in case of a failed transfer or cash-out. In his October 2026 speech, Piero Cipollone from the European Central Bank emphasized that one euro issued by a regulated bank should be exchangeable at par with a euro issued by another regulated bank.

For businesses, the concern is practical. Receiving money from a trading partner should not create additional hurdles simply because the payment originated on another bank's blockchain.

Consider a payment where a customer of Bank A makes a transfer of tokenized dollars to a supplier whose account is maintained at Bank B. First off, Bank B must ascertain whether it is willing to accept the payment. The process requires identification of the issuing bank, and also checking that the token and the transaction satisfy the criteria stipulated in the agreement between the two banks.

The banks then need to settle the payment. Depending on the particular system, the banks can settle the payment either by redemption of the token, use an existing payment rail, or settle via a shared platform involving the tokenized central bank money.

Bank B is allowed to credit the supplier as per the agreed rules once all necessary conditions are satisfied. Both institutions must also be able to reconcile the payment in their accounting systems.

The process of settling payments varies depending on the design. A shared platform may orchestrate several processes, while separate networks may require messages and transactions to pass between different systems.

The system needs to distinguish between a payment that has been submitted, one that has been accepted, and actual settlement of the payment in the system. It also needs to account for any separate redemption or account-crediting steps. A blockchain confirmation confirms that a transaction has been executed based on the rules of that particular network.It does not necessarily mean the receiving bank has accepted the deposit or credited its customer.

Bridges enable separate blockchains to transact and exchange either assets or information about the transaction. Some lock tokens on one network and create equivalent tokens on another, or employ any other techniques to perform transactions across networks. These tools can help move digital assets between blockchains; however, that will not automatically imply that the recipient bank will accept the deposits issued by another institution.

Suppose a bridge makes a representation of Bank A's token available on a second network. That token may be transferable there, but Bank B still has to know what kind of rights are included in this token. Can the holder redeem it with Bank A? Is it acceptable to Bank B? Who should take the responsibility if redemption is delayed or cannot be completed?

Creating another token does not resolve such issues.

At the same time, bridges also increase technical risks. Depending on their design, they may rely on smart contracts, validators, third-party messaging services or privileged operators. Any vulnerability or bug in a bridge’s logic could lead to unauthorized transfers or inconsistent records.

Banks therefore must take into account both technical aspects of linking two networks and financial obligations of the tokens. A bridge can help with the first without resolving the second.

The BIS Annual Economic Report 2026 discusses fragmentation across blockchain networks and the operational risks associated with connecting systems that use different rules and governance arrangements.

It is common for disputes to occur when there is a disagreement between the two systems about the transaction status. For instance, Bank A makes a payment request through its network but the confirmation fails to reach Bank B. Bank A detects a time-out in the communication and retries the request since it does not know whether the first request was made successfully.

When the receiving system considers both instructions separately, then the supplier might receive the amount twice. If the banks stop processing while they investigate, the funds may remain unavailable until they establish what happened.

The payment systems should have mechanisms that can cater for such situations. Idempotency enables the payment request to be retried without creating a duplicate payment request. Having a stable transaction identifier would help the receiving system to identify the retry request the same request rather than a new one. Atomic settlement can enable the two linked operations to succeed or fail simultaneously. Where the architecture supports it, this reduces the chances of one side of the payment being settled while the other one remains unsettled.

Atomic settlement is not a guarantee to avoid the above problem since some independent networks have transaction finality conditions which might not be able to coordinate each operation in a single transaction. The system must account for those limitations.

Transaction status also needs careful handling. A successful submitted transaction request does not mean a successful payment since there is a redemption or account crediting process after settlement. When the system uses each ledger update entry as confirmation of receipt of money from the receiving bank, it can report a successful transfer while the surrounding banking process is still incomplete.

When the outcome is uncertain, the banks need transaction records and reconciliation procedures to establish their respective positions. They also need an agreed process for resolving discrepancies without duplicating payments or losing track of the funds.

Two developments show how banks and financial institutions are approaching different parts of the problem.

In November 2025, JPMorgan rolled out its JPM Coin deposit token for institutional clients on Base. On October 19, 2026, the bank also announced the launch of JPM Coin on Ethereum. It makes it possible for eligible institutional clients to transfer JPM Coins within the Ethereum Virtual Machine ecosystem, which includes Base and Ethereum. It enables clients to use the bank's dollar-denominated deposit token on yet another public network.

For institutions already using Ethereum-based assets and applications, this can make it easier to use JPM Coin alongside their existing onchain activity. But supporting more than one blockchain does not guarantee the acceptance of the token by any other bank. JPM Coin is still tied to deposits in JPMorgan, and the token is limited to eligible institutional clients. The announcement illustrates the difference between making a token available on multiple networks and making it usable across unrelated banking relationships.

The BIS-led Project Agorá involves the application of more complex approaches to wholesale payments. It brings commercial bank deposits and tokenized central bank reserves on the same programmable platform. In May 2026, BIS published a report on the project’s prototype, which allowed atomic, multi-currency settlement across jurisdictions. Subsequently, the project team conducted the real-value testing in July 2026.

According to the BIS project overview, 28 financial institutions and central banks performed transactions totalling approximately CHF 800,000 across 17 scenarios. The test included the transactions related to both corporate and interbank payments, as well as those involving two currencies.

This testing revealed the necessity of operational activities needed for the platform. Participants used established payment-message standards, managed the issuance and redemption of tokenized deposits and reserves, and followed predefined procedures for executing transactions. The procedures included the fallback mechanism for situations when certain steps could not be completed as planned.

Those details are important because a payment platform must work with the systems banks already use. The ledger is not everything; the institution still needs to manage the corresponding funds, records, approvals, and exceptions.

Project Agorá provides evidence that coordinated settlement based on tokenized commercial bank deposits and central bank reserves can work in a controlled setting. It does not imply that all banks accept all other banks' deposit tokens. Wider adoption still depends on the legal, technical, and operational arrangements between participants.

Portability needs to be considered when designing the payment flow, rather than added later as a connection between blockchains. The system must identify the issuing bank and establish which receiving institutions can accept a particular token. It must define how the payment will be settled, when the receiving bank can credit the recipient, and what happens if one of those steps fails.

Redemption and reconciliation need similar attention. When a token is converted back into a conventional deposit, the token balance and the bank's corresponding records must remain consistent. The same applies when a payment uses tokenized central bank reserves or a shared settlement platform.

The system must also fit into existing banking operations. Compliance checks, fraud monitoring, accounting, treasury management, and customer account updates remain necessary when deposits are tokenized. Banks need to integrate these processes with the new infrastructure, including the procedures for delayed or rejected payments.

Testing should cover more than a successful transfer between two wallets. Engineers need to examine what happens when a receiving bank rejects an instruction, a message arrives late, a network becomes unavailable, or one institution records a transaction while another has yet to complete its part. Those tests help reveal whether the payment flow can recover from failures without duplicating transactions or leaving the institutions with inconsistent records.

JPM Coin's expansion to Ethereum gives institutional clients access to the deposit token on another public blockchain. Project Agorá has tested a shared platform that coordinates tokenized commercial bank deposits and central bank reserves for wholesale payments.

The approaches differ, but both show that moving money through programmable infrastructure involves more than recording transactions quickly.

A business receiving tokenized dollars needs to know whether its bank can accept them, how the payment will be settled, and when the funds will be available. If redemption requires a separate transfer or the banks cannot agree on the transaction's status, the speed of the original blockchain transaction offers limited help.

For tokenized deposits to work across banking relationships, institutions need arrangements that let them recognize the deposits, settle payments, and resolve failures. Until those arrangements are in place, the usefulness of a token will depend partly on which bank issued it and where the recipient needs to use it.

#9691. Teach your team to review AI code before you roll out an agent

Posted on Nov 18 • Originally published at chainofthought.show

It is easy to roll out an AI coding tool with a license and a Slack announcement and leave the training for later. Rizel Scarlett, a developer advocate at Block in our January 2025 episode, wants it the other way round. Companies already run new hires through security and harassment training, and she argues they might also need a "how to code with AI" training. Her baseline is short:

Like don't just check-in code, review it just as you would review a co worker's code and stuff like that.

Rizel Scarlett, on Chain of Thought ep 10

Here is how I'd turn that into a training plan and a merge checklist.

Scarlett works on Goose, Block's open-source, on-machine developer agent. It has a Rust back end and an Electron front end, and you can drive it from the terminal or the app. It connects to your file system and to other tools through Model Context Protocol servers, and Block collaborated with Anthropic on building out MCPs. She describes it as useful for almost any engineering task because it is so extensible.

That extensibility is the first thing to teach. Before anyone reviews code, they should know what the agent could touch while writing it: which directories, which MCP servers, which credentials sit in the environment. My concern is that a reviewer who only sees the diff may not see what else the agent read or ran. So the first session of the training is an inventory, and the first rule is to start a new agent in a scratch directory with no production data until the team has seen how it behaves.

Scarlett's favorite argument cuts against the "AI replaces juniors" line. When you are a junior developer, she says, you are scared to ask questions, and sometimes you do not understand the answer when you do. For her, starting out young and as a Black woman engineer added another layer of that fear.

But I'm like, if I had this when I was a junior developer, this would have made me so much more confident.

Rizel Scarlett, on Chain of Thought ep 10

Her point is that a junior can ask the tool why it chose something and why a method exists, as many times as they need. It works like a peer programmer. I would build the training around that use: ask why, check the answer against the docs, then write the test yourself. The agent explains; the developer still owns the proof.

This is also where prompting technique belongs. Show developers few-shot prompting, the prompt-level form of few-shot learning: put two or three examples of the code style you want into the prompt. Then show them that a well-prompted answer still needs review.

Scarlett's list is plain: keep writing tests, keep testing manually, and learn how hallucinations work and how to reduce them. I would teach it in four short sessions:

AI safety in a team setting starts with these habits. The guardrails go in before the agent runs, and the review happens before the merge.

A sketch of the pre-merge procedure you could print on the training's last slide:

Scarlett liked working with GitHub Copilot but did not know what was happening under the hood, and could not have as much influence as she wanted. At Block she can see feedback and push her own code to improve Goose, and so can community members. She also calls open source "authentic marketing": contributors talk about the project at conferences because they feel part of it.

For a team adopting an open-source agent, that has a practical side. You can read the code and propose fixes, and community contributions keep changing it. Treat each update like any other dependency bump: read the release notes, rerun your checks, and do not let an agent upgrade itself into production. The open source AI topic page has more conversations on how these projects grow.

  HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

Key Features

  • Provides suggestions for your topic clusters and related subjects
  • Integrates with all other HubSpot content tools to help you create a well-rounded content strategy

You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

Key features

It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.
