#9689. Responsible AI Change Control: 12 Triggers to Reopen an Approved Use Case

Posted on Nov 18 • Originally published at trust-vault.com

An AI approval is a decision about a particular system, purpose, population, data path, permissions, human workflow, and set of safeguards at a point in time. It is not a transferable badge that follows a model name forever. When one of those conditions changes, the practical question is not “Did the vendor update something?” It is “Could this change alter the system’s behavior, the people affected, the authority it exercises, or the evidence supporting the original decision?”

This guide provides a proportionate way to answer that question. It includes a twelve-trigger intake, a four-route review matrix, a change ledger, and a dependency-free Node.js validator. The asset is an operational decision aid: it does not classify systems under law, certify safety, or determine whether a regulatory conformity assessment is required.

The source article, security tooling notes, discusses responsible-AI principles at a high level. This Dev.to adaptation adds a narrower operating mechanism: how an owner decides whether an approved use case can continue after a model, prompt, data source, tool, or context changes.

Do not reopen a full approval for every typo, patch, or routine data refresh. Do reopen the decision when a change could affect a material risk assumption or a control the original approval relied on. Record the change, compare it with the approved baseline, test the affected pathway, and route the result to someone with authority to accept residual risk.

A lightweight route is enough when the change is reversible, isolated, low impact, and covered by a pre-approved operating envelope. A delta test is appropriate when one known component changes but purpose and authority remain the same. Cross-functional review is warranted when affected people, decisions, access, or external obligations may change. Pause the system when the change is unbounded, evidence is missing, a safeguard no longer works, or an incident indicates that the original risk model was wrong.

The European AI Act illustrates why precision matters. Article 43 addresses conformity assessment for specified high-risk AI systems and provides for a new assessment in the event of a substantial modification, with an exception for certain changes predetermined and documented. Article 72 describes post-market monitoring obligations for providers of high-risk systems. These scoped provisions do not establish a general rule that every business must use this exact checklist. Apply the relevant law to the actual role, system, intended purpose, and current consolidated text; obtain qualified legal advice where needed. The framework below is voluntary internal control. Article 43 · Article 72.

The distinction matters because both extremes create avoidable risk. If every adjustment triggers a committee, teams learn to route changes around governance or delay useful fixes. If no change ever reopens the decision, a narrow approval can silently become permission for a different system. A practical process must separate “the thing changed” from “the approved risk assumptions changed.”

Practitioner discussions surface operational questions that policy summaries do not answer: who may approve a new source document; how can an owner find the exact instruction version behind a response; who investigates a reported wrong answer; what happens when a source is withdrawn; and whether connecting an agent to a new tool changes human control. These are configuration, ownership, and evidence questions.

The AI Security Institute’s evaluation work describes pre-deployment and post-deployment testing and identifies significant model updates, new tools, fine-tuning, longer context windows, and newly available capabilities as possible reasons to test. It also cautions that evaluations are snapshots and do not certify a system as safe. This supports a change-trigger approach, but it does not prescribe this article’s thresholds or prove that a particular corporate process will prevent harm. AISI’s evaluation lessons.

A change cannot be assessed against a vague statement such as “AI assistant for operations.” Write a baseline that identifies the intended purpose, users, affected people, decisions supported, model and provider identifiers, prompt or policy version, input and retrieval sources, tools and permissions, deployment surface, human checkpoints, monitoring signals, known limitations, and the owner who can stop the system.

For each item, record enough detail to reproduce the decision. A model label alone may not be sufficient if the provider can update the underlying model behind a stable alias. “Company documents” is not enough if the retrieval index contains customer contracts, public help pages, and unreviewed uploads. “Human oversight” is not meaningful unless the record says which human sees what, at what point, with which authority, and what happens when that person rejects or cannot review an output.

A baseline should distinguish what approval explicitly tested from what it merely assumed. If tests covered normal requests but no adversarial documents, that boundary matters. If a human checked only a sample, do not describe the control as universal review. If a decision-maker approved read-only retrieval, that approval does not automatically include sending emails or changing records.

The ledger below should point to immutable or versioned artifacts where possible: a model identifier, prompt commit, dataset snapshot, connector scope, test run, and approval record. Store sensitive material under the organization’s access and retention rules; the purpose is traceability, not creating a second uncontrolled data repository.

These triggers are prompts for assessment, not automatic verdicts. A “yes” means document the delta and choose a route; it does not necessarily mean stop or convene a committee.

The table is intentionally broader than a legal checklist. A switch from one model version to another might be routine in a low-impact summarizer if the supplier’s documented update process is inside the approved envelope and a regression suite passes. The same model change may require more serious review when it affects a tool-using agent that can send customer communications. The relevant delta is not only “model changed”; it is “the evidence and authority in this use case may no longer match.”

Capture provider, endpoint, model identifier, version date, fallback behavior, region where relevant, and documented update policy. Ask whether the version is pinned or whether a stable alias can resolve to a new model without notice. Compare representative tasks and failure cases instead of relying only on a vendor’s general capability statement.

A provider change can affect output style, refusal behavior, latency, tool calling, or prompt interpretation. It can also change contractual data handling or incident notification. Do not infer that every model change is high risk; do not infer that a familiar product name means nothing changed. If the provider cannot disclose a version, record that limitation and compensate with repeatable black-box evaluation proportionate to use.

Prompts and system instructions often encode scope decisions: who the system serves, what counts as success, what it must never do, when it must abstain, and which source wins in a conflict. A stylistic rewrite can be minor; a sentence permitting the assistant to “complete the task” may be material if it changes a draft-only agent into one that sends the draft.

Diff versions and map each changed instruction to the control it affects. A reviewer should tell whether the change alters the allowed objective, refusal behavior, confidence language, escalation requirement, or action boundary. Test the changed boundary directly. A generic “works as expected” prompt run does not demonstrate that a newly permitted behavior is contained.

A corpus update can change answers without changing the model. Track source owner, inclusion rules, refresh schedule, withdrawal process, and last successful indexing time. Changes to source authority, version, or population may matter more than the number of new files. An old policy removed from search, a new third-party document, or a public page copied into a private index can reverse the answer.

Ask whether the source is authoritative for the question, current for the relevant date, and appropriate for the audience. Verify that citations shown to the user point to the retrieved material. If access controls differ across documents, confirm that retrieval cannot expose one user’s content to another. A refresh that replaces a document with a newer edition may fit a routine envelope; adding unreviewed uploads to a system used for contractual advice may not.

Record new input fields and their purpose. The question is not only whether an input contains personal data; it is whether the data changes what the system can infer, retain, share, or decide. A workflow that previously processed anonymized product metadata may take on a different risk profile when free-text customer messages are added.

New tools can change an AI system from an information source into an actor. Compare permission scopes and reachable objects, not only the connector name. Read-only calendar access, write access to the calendar, and permission to send an invitation are different authorities. A browser or code execution tool can also expose data or create side effects.

Use least privilege and separate capabilities where possible. Test that prohibited actions fail closed, that approvals bind to the exact pending action, and that retries cannot repeat a side effect. If a change adds a write or external communication permission, require a route that examines the affected action and human checkpoint. Never assume that a user’s broad approval of an agent means it may take every action exposed by a connector.

A system approved for trained internal analysts may behave differently in a public self-service flow. Users may have different language needs, ability to detect errors, incentive to rely, or access to recourse. People affected by a system may not be the same people operating it. Record both groups and what each can see or challenge.

A change in audience should trigger a review of instructions, accessibility, disclosures, support, escalation, and the test population. Sample cases should represent the new users and the decisions they face. Avoid turning a demographic label into a proxy for risk; explain the mechanism by which the audience change could matter. If the use case is narrow and the interface prevents reliance beyond its scope, a targeted design check may suffice instead of a full governance reset.

Distinguish assistance from determination. Summarizing a document, suggesting a next step, ranking candidates, setting a price, routing a complaint, and deciding eligibility are different functions. A new scoring or recommendation layer may increase reliance even if the interface still calls the output “advice.”

Map output to the real workflow: who sees it, what action follows, whether the person can disagree, and whether alternatives remain available. Check if the system now influences an outcome about a person or organization in a way absent from the approved use case. A human clicking the final button does not alone establish meaningful oversight. The reviewer needs evidence that the person has time, information, authority, and a practical route to override.

Human oversight is a system component. If a reviewer is removed, moved later in the process, given less context, or measured only on speed, the control may have changed even though the model did not. Track who reviews, what evidence they receive, which outputs are automatically acted on, and what conditions require escalation.

Test realistic workload conditions, including ambiguous cases and a reviewer who lacks a required source. A “human in the loop” label is not proof that a person can catch an error. If the reviewer cannot distinguish generated content from sourced facts, or cannot stop an external action, record that gap. Conversely, an interface change that makes sources and uncertainty clearer may lower risk, but still warrants a short usability check before treating the original approval as current.

The same model can create different effects in a low-volume internal research tool and a high-volume customer channel. Geography, timing, integration, batch size, and service expectations can change reliance and the impact of failure. A system used only during staffed hours may behave differently when it handles requests overnight without an available reviewer.

Compare actual operating conditions with those tested. Include peak loads, timeouts, degraded dependencies, fallback routes, and cross-channel identity. If a tool is embedded into a workflow, users may stop seeing where its suggestion ends and a business decision begins. Record surrounding product changes as part of the AI system’s context; an unchanged model can still participate in a changed decision.

A complaint, near miss, unexpected output, drift alert, security event, or provider notice is a change signal about the evidence base. It may not mean the system changed; it may mean the team learned that original assumptions were incomplete. Record the report, affected version, exposure window, severity, whether a person or external system was affected, and what evidence is preserved.

The external environment can change conditions for continued use. Relevant changes may include regulation, a sector rule, a contract, a data-processing term, a customer commitment, or a standard incorporated into policy. Do not treat a news headline as a legal determination. Ask the responsible legal or compliance owner whether the change applies to this organization, role, system, and use.

The EU AI Act source pages demonstrate why scope matters. Article 43 speaks to conformity assessment for high-risk systems and substantial modifications; Article 72 concerns post-market monitoring by providers for high-risk systems. The Act has role-specific and system-specific provisions, and the Service Desk identifies that its displayed text follows a consolidated regulation dated 27 July 2026. A generic internal ledger may organize evidence, but it is not the statutory assessment or monitoring plan. Consult the current operative text and qualified counsel. Article 43 and its consolidation note · Article 72.

The output of intake should be a route with an owner, evidence, and decision date. These are operational recommendations, not legal risk classifications. Map terms such as “low” or “high” to the organization’s own risk framework.

The route follows potential consequence and uncertainty, not how difficult the change is to describe. If a change expands access and affects a consequential decision, do not split it into two “small” tickets to avoid review. Assess the combined delta.

Route A should be normal for controlled maintenance, but the basis still needs a short record. Route B should specify what passed or failed, not simply say “tested.” Route C should identify people with decision authority, not collect attendees without ownership. Route D is not punishment. It prevents further exposure while the team learns what changed and whether the old control still works.

A useful ledger is not a narrative meeting note. It is a compact record connecting the approved state to the proposed state and explaining why the chosen route is proportionate. Store one record per change event, then link to tests, approvals, incidents, and artifacts. Do not overwrite the prior baseline; create a new version so a reviewer can reconstruct which configuration was approved at a particular time.

A minimal record includes system ID; use-case ID; change ID; date detected; reporter; owner; baseline version; proposed version; trigger IDs; changed fields; affected people and workflows; expected benefit; plausible failure path; data and permission delta; route; test plan; test result; reviewer; residual risk; rollback; release decision; and next review signal. For each field, define an accepted value such as “unknown” rather than allowing empty fields to be misread as “not applicable.”

A synthetic example exposes the reasoning. An internal policy assistant has approval for read-only access to two versioned policy collections. A team proposes adding a third-party benefits guide and enabling a ticket-creation tool. The source change triggers retrieval and source-authority review. The connector triggers tool and permission review. The combined change is not a simple corpus refresh because the assistant can now create a workflow artifact. The team records the new source’s owner and date, verifies attribution, tests whether unsupported advice is escalated, checks that the ticket tool cannot submit without the designated reviewer, and routes the change to cross-functional review. This is a worked synthetic scenario, not a report of a real deployment.

A ledger entry should capture a decision even when the conclusion is “no material delta.” The rationale makes that conclusion auditable. For example: “The provider rotated a patch version under the documented update process; endpoint, data terms, capabilities used, prompt, tools, population, and tested tasks were unchanged; the regression suite passed; rollback is available.” That is better than “minor update” because it shows what the owner actually checked.

Teams often ask for a single number to automate routing. A score can help triage work, but it should not be presented as a probability of harm or a compliance rating. The following ordinal rubric is a prioritization prompt only. Score six dimensions from zero to two: zero means unchanged or demonstrably contained; one means a bounded difference needs a targeted check; two means a material or unknown change. The dimensions are affected people, decision authority, data sensitivity, external action, control strength, and uncertainty. The total is not validated; it is a reminder to consider more than model identity.

Use it only with explicit override rules. Any credible incident, failed safeguard, unauthorized action, unknown permission expansion, or change to a decision affecting people routes at least to cross-functional review regardless of the sum. A high total can trigger review; a low total cannot guarantee safety. If several dimensions are unknown, gather evidence instead of assigning zero.

Do not tune a score until it produces the desired number of approvals. If the organization needs a quantitative risk method, define it separately with rationale, thresholds, calibration evidence, and governance ownership. This table is deliberately not calibrated against incident rates and makes no empirical predictive claim.

A delta test starts with the failure path implied by the trigger. If retrieval changed, test whether the assistant now finds outdated, conflicting, or unauthorized material. If a connector gained write access, test denied actions, approval binding, replay, retries, identity, and rollback. If the model changed, test existing high-risk and boundary cases against the new version and compare results with the same rubric.

Keep stable test cases where possible. A version comparison only makes sense if task, inputs, scoring, and relevant environment are held constant or their differences are documented. Add cases when the change reveals a new risk path; do not silently replace old cases with easier ones. Record test date, model and configuration identifiers, prompt versions, dataset snapshot, evaluation owner, grader method, known exclusions, and confidence limits.

Automated tests can cover many cases but may not reflect real use. Human evaluation may be slower and itself inconsistent. AISI’s published work explains both the value and limitations of evaluation approaches, including that automated evaluations do not mirror real-world usage and evaluation methods remain an evolving science. A release packet can combine deterministic regression, targeted human review, and monitored rollout, with each method tied to a question. None alone establishes that a system is safe. AISI on evaluation timing and method limits.

For a live system, consider staged exposure when feasible: internal test, limited cohort, monitored release, then broader access after defined signals remain within the approved envelope. Staging is not an excuse to expose people to known failures. Establish stop conditions before rollout and ensure the monitor can halt the system.

The dependency-free Node.js example checks record completeness and route consistency. It does not inspect model behavior, determine legal obligations, or certify a change. It catches missing metadata and prevents an intake from being silently marked “record only” when fields show an escalation trigger. Adapt the policy, review it with responsible owners, and keep it versioned with the ledger schema.

The sample is synthetic. Its categories and trigger IDs are design choices in this proposed protocol; they were not derived from measured deployments. The validator’s output indicates only whether the submitted record satisfies these example rules.

A successful output means only that this record meets the example schema and escalation floor. It does not mean the source was appropriate, the test adequate, the reviewer independent, or the deployment compliant with law. The dangerous misuse of a validator is to turn syntactic completeness into substantive assurance.

Use code review for policy changes to the validator. If someone removes the tool-permission trigger from the escalation set, that is itself a governance change. Keep fixtures for an ordinary patch, bounded retrieval update, expanded write permission, reported incident, and unknown provider change. A test that verifies only the happy path cannot show that the process catches the boundaries it was created to enforce.

A practical review encounters incomplete provider notices, unavailable model version IDs, noisy user reports, undocumented legacy prompts, and missing baselines. The record should make uncertainty visible instead of converting it into implied approval. State what is known, inferred, and unknown. Name the evidence that would resolve each unknown and the person responsible for obtaining it.

Where a provider does not expose a stable build, capture the endpoint, observed date, provider notice, and a repeatable behavioral fingerprint from controlled tasks. Do not call that fingerprint a model identity. It is an observation that may help identify behavioral change, not a substitute for provenance. If observations differ, investigate provider, prompt, retrieval state, and runtime context before attributing the difference to the model.

When an incident report is ambiguous, preserve the original report, avoid sharing unnecessary personal data, and ask a trained reviewer to classify it. Separate “the model produced a wrong answer” from “a person relied on it,” “a tool executed it,” and “an adverse outcome followed.” These are distinct facts. Review can be urgent before every fact is known; containment can reflect exposure and plausible harm while root-cause conclusions wait for evidence.

If the baseline is absent, reconstruct it from source control, deployment logs, provider history, tickets, and approval notes. Mark reconstructed elements as reconstructed, state date and confidence, and do not invent original scope. Until a minimum baseline exists, a bounded pause or restricted operation is safest when the use case can affect people or external systems. For a low-impact internal research aid, a short time-boxed reconstruction may be proportionate.

Review everything as if it were a new system. This consumes review capacity and teaches teams that governance is a delay. A patch inside a documented, tested envelope should normally receive a recorded decision and relevant regression result. Escalate when evidence points to a changed risk assumption, not because the release number changed.

Treat a stable name as proof of stability. An alias can point to different behavior; an unchanged product brand can hide a new source or permission. Record evidence at the component and workflow level. Where exact versioning is unavailable, state the limit and compensate with a repeatable evaluation.

Call a prompt edit “just copy.” A wording change can alter objectives, refusal boundaries, or tool selection. Compare meaning and test the boundary. Conversely, many prompt edits really are cosmetic. Review should identify the semantic delta, not assume that every prompt change is harmless or high risk.

Treat a human click as meaningful oversight. A hurried reviewer who sees only a final answer and cannot inspect evidence may not provide an effective control. Test what the reviewer sees and can do. If review is one of the approval’s safety assumptions, preserve evidence that it functions in the actual workflow.

Use a single score as the decision. A sum can hide one severe dimension behind several zeros. Preserve hard overrides and explain why the route is appropriate. Scores direct attention; accountable owners make the decision.

Confuse regulatory scope with internal good practice. A useful ledger does not make an organization a provider, classify a system as high-risk, complete conformity assessment, or discharge a monitoring obligation. The AI Act Service Desk says its summaries are explanatory and not legally binding; its pages identify the consolidated text date. Consult operative text and qualified counsel for scope questions.

Measure only model output. A tool-using system can cause harm through access and action even if wording looks acceptable. Test permission boundaries, side effects, approval binding, data exposure, and failure recovery. Output-quality tests are necessary but insufficient for an agent.

Ignore the source of a report. User complaints, automated monitoring, provider notices, and red-team findings have different coverage and incentives. Preserve source and context. Do not treat a quiet dashboard as proof that users experienced no failures.

Keep a stale approval because no incident occurred. Absence of a report can mean low exposure, weak monitoring, or no practical reporting path. Ask whether monitoring could observe the relevant failure and whether people could report it. Do not claim “no incidents” unless the observation process supports that statement.

Escalate every source refresh. A known owner replacing an expired policy with its approved successor may be within the intended envelope. The decision still needs evidence that the new version is authoritative, indexed, access-controlled, and covered by regression cases. The route can be a record or delta test; ceremony is not a substitute for a source check.

Run trigger intake before a material release, when a provider announces an update, after a safety or security event, when a source is added or withdrawn, and during periodic monitoring. A calendar review can detect slow drift, but it cannot replace event-driven intake. Conversely, every routine refresh should not wait for a quarterly committee if it sits inside a tested scope.

Make submissions easy. Ask what changed; which system and use case; when; who requested it; which baseline fields changed; whether people, data, access, decisions, or obligations are affected; whether incident evidence exists; what tests are available; how to roll back; and who is accountable. Pre-fill data from deployment pipelines where possible, so process does not rely on an operator remembering every identifier.

Measure process performance carefully. Useful operational measures include time from detected change to triage, proportion of records with a traceable baseline, proportion of tests covering stated risk pathways, and releases rolled back after a guardrail failed. These describe control process, not system safety. Avoid targets that reward closing changes quickly or push teams to lower their route. Pair speed measures with a review of decision quality and exceptions.

This guide was prepared on 18 November 2026. The original asset consists of a twelve-trigger intake, four review routes, a six-dimension ordinal prompt for triage, a synthetic change scenario, and a small dependency-free JavaScript validator. The counts of triggers, routes, and dimensions are design choices in this proposed protocol. They are not study results, performance benchmarks, or statistics about AI incidents.

The synthetic case uses invented system names, identifiers, and evidence references. No production system, model, vendor, prompt, customer record, or evaluation result was tested for this article. The Node.js sample was reviewed as an example of input validation logic but has not been run against an organization’s governance system. Teams should adapt and test it before use.

The research path compared a general responsible-AI page with official AI Act text, a public evaluation institute’s discussion of evaluation timing, an analyst’s governance commentary, and practitioner questions about source ownership, change triggers, and incorrect outputs. A targeted video search did not return a clearly relevant expert video that added evidence beyond the written primary sources, so no video claim is used. This article does not estimate market adoption, incident frequency, audit effectiveness, or legal compliance.

The official sources are narrow. Article 43 concerns conformity assessment for specified high-risk AI systems; Article 72 concerns post-market monitoring by providers of high-risk systems. The Service Desk says the displayed text follows a consolidated regulation as of 27 July 2026 and that its summaries are not legally binding. ECAS’s page discusses AI data-center conditions rather than change-control outcomes; it supports only the narrow point about recording infrastructure context. AISI says evaluation science is evolving and cautions against treating evaluations as safety certification. Those limits shape the recommendations above.

Before submitting a change for approval, ask:

A good change-control process is not the one that produces the most approvals. It preserves the reasons an approval was granted, detects when those reasons may no longer hold, and responds at a pace proportionate to exposure. The ledger makes that decision inspectable. The tests make the reasoning concrete. The accountable owner decides whether the system remains inside its approved envelope, needs another review, or must pause.

#9688. Cranberry Cream Cheese Spread

Of all the incredible dips we’ve created over the years, our cranberry whipped feta dip is an internet and personal favorite—so much so that I just had to come back with an equally luxurious variation: this cranberry-topped whipped cream cheese spread. With the holiday party season just around the corner, this spread is begging to be included in your party spread. Plus, it's as easy to make as it is delicious—a tangy, sweet cranberry sauce gets finished with brandy, then is spooned atop a lemony whipped cream cheese for a guaranteed winning combo.

Fresh Or Frozen Cranberries? I used both while testing, and they both work interchangeably. I found the fresh cranberries broke down a little more than frozen, so it depends on whether or not you’re looking for more or less texture in your sauce.

What temperature should the cream cheese be? Make sure the cream cheese is chilled and softened but not super cold. It should be somewhat pliable when whipping to avoid lumps; this will ensure the mixture is light and airy. A little heavy cream will loosen the mixture if it's too thick.

The lemon zest: I found that the cream cheese layer needed a little more oomph. If you get a bite of cream cheese on a cracker, it shouldn’t be one-dimensional. Adding a touch of lemon zest makes it more palatable.

Storage:Store the cream cheese spread, with or without cranberry sauce, in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.

#9687. AI Agents Could Drive the Next Open Source Software Revolution

Building tomorrow's software today. AI-powered mobile apps • Carrier-grade infrastructure • Open source security • Hack

Building tomorrow's software today. AI-powered mobile apps • Carrier-grade infrastructure • Open source security • Hack

Building tomorrow's software today. AI-powered mobile apps • Carrier-grade infrastructure • Open source security • Hack

As coding tools improve, software companies will need more than a polished interface to defend their business. Open source communities will need better coordination, too.

Imagine a team paying for a workflow tool that almost fits its needs. An open source alternative exists, but it lacks an integration, has confusing documentation, and needs a better interface. Those gaps are small enough to describe and large enough to keep the team paying.

If AI coding agents help contributors close those gaps at a reasonable cost, the decision changes. That is the opportunity I see for open source: more projects becoming practical alternatives to the software people rent today.

My bet is that one of AI's biggest effects on software will come from communities improving shared tools. The difficult part is turning generated code into something people can trust.

There is evidence that AI assistance can accelerate some coding tasks. In a controlled experiment published in 2023, developers using GitHub Copilot completed a JavaScript HTTP server task 55.8% faster than the control group. That result concerned one bounded task with a coding assistant, so it cannot establish the economics of maintaining an entire product.

Other research shows why that distinction matters. METR's early-2025 randomized trial involved 16 experienced open-source developers completing 246 tasks in repositories they knew well. Allowing AI tools increased completion time by 19%.

In a February 2026 follow-up, METR said newer tools likely provided greater benefits, but selection effects and difficulties measuring time made its new results unreliable for estimating the size of those gains. The 2025 slowdown is not a verdict on every tool or workflow, and the follow-up is not proof of a universal speedup.

For open source, I would focus on specific, reviewable work: improving an installation guide, reproducing a bug, adding a missing integration, or testing an edge case. Agents could help contributors tackle these tasks, provided someone understands the changes and checks the result.

The useful measure is how much accepted, working improvement a project gains for the time its contributors and maintainers spend.

Developers have organized alternatives when vendors changed the terms of widely used software.

In August 2023, HashiCorp announced a move to the Business Source License for future releases of products including Terraform. The Linux Foundation announced OpenTofu, a community fork of the previously open source Terraform code, in September 2023. HashiCorp's announcement and the OpenTofu launch announcement document that sequence.

In March 2024, Redis announced that releases starting with Redis 7.4 would use the source-available RSALv2 and SSPLv1 licenses. Later that month, the Linux Foundation announced Valkey, continuing development from Redis 7.2.4 under the BSD 3-clause license, with support from companies including AWS and Google Cloud. Redis's announcement and the Valkey launch announcement explain the changes.

Redis subsequently added AGPLv3 as an open-source licensing option with Redis 8 in May 2025. Redis's AGPLv3 announcement makes that later change explicit.

These examples demonstrate the importance of licensing, governance, and organized contributors. They do not establish that AI agents created or sustained these forks. My prediction is that better coding tools could reduce some of the implementation work required for future community responses. Funding and experienced maintainers would still matter.

If competitors can reproduce more of your product's visible features, ask what customers would still need from your company.

That might be specialized data, reliable infrastructure, access to payment or communications networks, operational expertise, or a service customers trust. A well-documented API can make those capabilities useful across many interfaces and workflows.

Stripe's payment APIs and Twilio's communications APIs illustrate this model: developers can build their own applications around services supplied by another company. Stripe's Payment Intents documentation and Twilio's API overview show how those services are exposed.

I expect more companies to benefit from letting developers build interfaces and integrations around their services, including open-source ones. An API alone offers little protection, though. Its value depends on the capability behind it, its reliability, and the terms under which developers can use it.

There is also a tradeoff for users. An open source interface built on a proprietary API still depends on that provider's pricing and availability. Owning the front end does not mean owning the whole stack.

I expect the strongest pressure on products whose main advantage is a modest feature set or interface that competitors can reproduce without unusual resources. Lower implementation costs could make those markets more crowded.

Even there, replacing a product involves more than matching its screens. Migration, integrations, accessibility, support, and the confidence to entrust it with real work all affect the decision.

Companies with valuable data, deep domain knowledge, dependable operations, or strong networks may be better positioned. They will still have to earn their customers' business. Neither a proprietary codebase nor an open source license guarantees a good product.

There are several reasons this shift could be slower or narrower than I expect.

These are conditions the thesis has to survive. Open source gains ground only where the complete alternative, including the work of operating it, makes sense for users.

Lowering the effort required to start a project could also increase the number of overlapping, unfinished tools. If contributors repeatedly rebuild the same basics, the ecosystem may gain repositories without gaining dependable alternatives.

Experimentation has value. The danger is spreading maintenance effort across more projects than a community can support. A working prototype is a useful beginning, but users need a reason to believe it will still work after the next dependency update.

My preferred response is a simple set of habits.

Agents could help contributors navigate unfamiliar code and prepare changes. The responsibility for a useful contribution remains with the person submitting it.

I think AI coding agents could help open source compete across more of the software stack. The opportunity is substantial, but it depends on communities turning assistance into sustained improvements and companies delivering value customers cannot easily replace.

The question I would ask before starting another repository is simple: could this same effort make an existing project good enough for more people to use?

Which paid tool would you consider replacing with an open-source alternative, and what would that alternative need to earn your trust?

#9686. Cutting trial-checkout abandonment on a subscription SaaS (61% to 68.5%)

Posted on Nov 18 • Originally published at pkushal.com.np

The whole fix in one picture: a $0 trial that asked for about ten fields, cut to three or one click.

The funnel already worked. Organic traffic was healthy and a steady trickle of trials converted every week. The problem sat at the very end: of the people who actually began the trial checkout, a large share never finished. No new traffic, no price change, no product rebuild was needed. The friction was almost entirely in the form itself, and most of it was a setting that could be switched off.

The context The client runs a subscription apparel-mockup platform: users browse a large library of garment mockups, drop their own artwork onto a blank, and export a high-resolution product image. It is monetised with a 7-day free trial that rolls into a monthly plan, built on WordPress with MemberPress handling membership and checkout, and Stripe and PayPal as the payment gateways.

What I set out to achieve One focused goal: lift the rate at which people who start the trial checkout actually complete it. No new traffic, no price change, no product rebuild. Just remove whatever was making ready-to-sign-up users give up at the form.

Audited the live checkout field by field To start a $0 trial, the form asked for about ten inputs: email, password, confirm password, then a full billing address (name, two address lines, city, country, state, postcode), and finally card or PayPal. There was no Google or social signup. Asking someone to type a full postal address and invent a password to begin a free trial is a textbook abandonment driver, and the data agreed.

Traced the friction to platform defaults, not custom code The important realisation was that none of this needed a rebuild. In MemberPress, the billing-address fields are a native setting under Settings > Fields, and they are only forced when the store collects tax. The password and confirm fields can be removed natively too, with MemberPress auto-generating a password and emailing a set-password link. Google signup was the only piece needing a small social-login add-on. So the heavy, scary form was mostly a stack default that could be switched off, not a hard constraint.

Specced the change so the developer could ship it cleanly I wrote the exact plan: add Continue with Google, remove the billing-address block, switch card capture to the Stripe Payment Element so Stripe collects only the minimum the card network needs, and keep the existing GA4 and GTM events firing so the result stayed measurable. The target was email plus card, around three visible inputs, or one click with Google.

The hurdles, and how I got past them “Do we even need the billing address, or is removing it custom work?”

Download the Medium app I verified it against MemberPress’s own documentation rather than guessing: address fields are a native toggle and are only mandatory when tax is being collected. I confirmed the store did not collect tax, which meant the whole block could be hidden with a setting, no custom code. That turned a nervous “can we even do this” into a five-minute change.

Fine, and native. I showed the Disable Password Fields option that emails a set-password link after checkout, and the fallback of keeping a single password field but dropping the redundant "confirm" box with a show/hide toggle. The client kept control of the decision while every option stayed low-friction.

Staging was locked behind HTTP basic auth, so I could not log into it.

I could not drive the staging environment myself, so I grounded every recommendation in the platform documentation, the public production pages and the GA4 data, and handed the developer a precise click-path to apply and verify. The change shipped without me ever needing their admin.

The rebuild quietly changed the analytics event schema.

After launch, new signup events began firing that did not exist before, which made a naive before and after count misleading. I anchored the headline on the completion rate, which is robust to volume and schema shifts, and I flagged the schema change openly rather than cherry-picking a flattering absolute number.

The result Across the four weeks after launch, measured on the same GA4 funnel: of the people who began the trial checkout, 124 of 203 completed before the change and 89 of 130 after. As rates, completion rose from 61.1% to 68.5%, and abandonment fell from about 39% to 31%.

Completion rate up roughly seven points, a relative drop of about a fifth in abandonment, from a signup-flow change alone.

Fewer fields and a one-click option at the exact moment of decision meant more of the people who had already chosen to sign up actually got through the door.

What I was honest about: the limits I did not claim “more sales”. In the measured window, absolute purchases actually fell, because fewer people reached checkout at all (total traffic was down around 15%). The honest, defensible win is the completion rate, which normalises for volume and still improved clearly. I also flagged that the rebuild changed the event schema, so this is an early, directional read; a longer, stable window with the new tracking settled would firm it up further. Reporting the rate, caveats included, is more useful to the client than a flattering number that would not survive scrutiny.

What I would do next Two fast-follows have since shipped: reassurance microcopy at the card step (cancel anytime, money-back guarantee) and a mobile pass on the trimmed form. The next move is upstream, and waits only on a clean month of the new tracking: the product pages still gate the mockup before a visitor has felt any value, so the larger gain is in how the product earns the signup in the first place. The checkout was the fastest, lowest-risk win; the deeper one is a value-first path into the tool.

The heavy form was never a hard requirement. It was a default nobody had turned off, standing between ready-to-sign-up users and the product.

#9684. Mashed Potatoes

No holiday table—or really any dinner table, for that matter—is truly complete without a substantial side of creamy, buttery mashed potatoes. While it may seem like simple, classic comfort food, there are a few ways to take mashed potatoes from good to great. That's why we retested this recipe again and again until we achieved potato perfection.

What People Are Saying:"So good! I don’t typically like sour cream on its own but it was a huge improvement for basic mashed potatoes. Will definitely be making this again." – PurpleStrawberry

"Easily my go-to mashed potato recipe. I've made it for Thanksgiving, and got requests to make it again. It's so good, doesn't even need gravy." – kitkat123

Really, the only chopping you'll have to do is cut up the potatoes. I do suggest peeling them (more on that later), and be sure to try to cut the potatoes into equal-sized pieces so they cook evenly. Around 1" chunks are ideal. Time to cook 'em! In testing, I found that covering the potatoes with cold water first yields the best consistency and ensures the potatoes don't become too mushy. Don't forget to add a pinch of salt to the water! Let the potatoes cook until softened—the best way to test is to use a paring knife and make sure it can be inserted with no resistance. This should take about 20 minutes. Make sure to drain when they're done so they don't overcook.

Now comes the fun part: Mashing the potatoes until smooth. You can use a masher, a ricer, or even a handheld mixer for this step. I think the smoother, the better, but you do you, of course.

On to what makes these potatoes the best ever: Heat up some whole milk and butter until the butter is melted in a pot.

Then, pour over the still-warm potatoes and mix to combine. Then add the sour cream, some salt, and pepper, and you're basically good to go! Mix everything well, transfer to your prettiest serving bowl, and proceed with the finishing touches: a couple of pieces of butter to melt into the potatoes, plus fresh parsley for some color and brightness. Brace yourself for the compliments.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

If you have any leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for a max of 3 to 4 days. With all of our recipes to transform your creamy leftover mashed potatoes—like fried mashed potato balls, potato rolls, waffles... we doubt they'll even last that long.

#9682. Secure Amazon Bedrock access: who calls which model, under which identity?

Posted on Nov 18 • Originally published at span.observer

On a Thursday the Bedrock bill doubles and nobody can say which team called which model. The AWS logs show one shared role, not a person or an application. That scenario is the simplest test of secure Amazon Bedrock access: can you answer, after the fact, « who called what, under which identity, and at what cost »?

In November 2025 AWS and Dynatrace published a reference pattern for this: a gateway placed in front of Bedrock. Dynatrace’s post explains the idea; the technical detail lives in an AWS code sample under the MIT-0 licence. Dynatrace presents the pattern as coming from its own generative AI workloads (vendor post).

This article does not tour the product. It follows an operations decision: what should your team check before ten teams call Bedrock through the same door? It is separate from our piece on vulnerable AI services, which is about software components, not identity.

A note on honesty: span.observer has not deployed this pattern. The facts come from the Dynatrace post, the AWS architecture post (only partly readable) and the repository’s CloudFormation file, read as published. The identity model and the Dynatrace-side tracking remain for you to verify.

Without an intermediary, each application signs its own requests with AWS credentials. Three problems follow, which the Dynatrace post sums up: models that anyone holding credentials can invoke, audit evidence that is hard to produce, and developers who handle request signing themselves.

The gateway moves the question. The client presents a token from your identity system; the gateway checks it, signs the request on its behalf, then forwards it to Bedrock. The client keeps the usual AWS SDK (Boto3 in the sample). According to the AWS sample, you disable client-side signing and add an aws-endpoint-prefix header, plus an optional bearer token.

The post also cites quotas and throttling, per-tenant usage tracking, and no extra code when Bedrock adds a feature. The repository does not describe how those are implemented: usage plans appear only as suggested enhancements. Treat them as goals, not shipped features.

The path has four stages. Each is a decision point and a place to leave a trace.

An optional Route 53 piece gives the gateway its own domain name. The integration Lambda does not know Bedrock’s APIs one by one: it passes requests through. That avoids rewriting the gateway for every new feature, but it also leaves the gateway blind to content.

The bedrock-llm-gateway.yaml file is a starting point, not a finished solution. Three details found in the file (read on 11 November 2026) deserve a decision before production.

First, one parameter opens or closes the door.

The default is a PRIVATE endpoint (reachable from a VPC) with the authorizer on. A rule rejects a REGIONAL deployment without an authorizer. However, EnableAuthorizer: false remains possible on a private endpoint: the repository reserves it for testing, but nothing stops someone forgetting it.

Second, identity is not supplied. The shipped authorizer is a stub that denies everything.

Two lines matter for traceability. The authorizer result is cached for 300 seconds, so a revoked token can still pass for five minutes. And the stub hard-codes the principal as 'user': if you keep it and only replace the token test, all your callers will look like one. Return the real identity (team, application or user) in principalId.

Third, the integration Lambda’s permissions are broad.

The role gets the managed policy AmazonBedrockFullAccess. The repository itself recommends least privilege. Since every call goes through this role, Bedrock sees the role, not the caller: restrict the allowed models, and do not rely on Bedrock’s own logs alone to tell your teams apart.

One last point: the file we read configures neither access logs nor tracing on the API stage. Tracking is yours to build.

Dynatrace’s post says that observability of Bedrock workloads gives continuous insight into performance, reliability and cost, and helps confirm that controls stay effective. It does not say how to wire it, and we have not tested it. What follows is the author’s proposal, not from the post.

From an SRE viewpoint, a gateway adds a link: give it its own availability and latency SLO, separate from Bedrock’s, otherwise an authorizer outage will look like a model outage. The 300-second timeout on the integration Lambda, read in the file, suggests long responses fit; the AWS post also mentions streaming, which we did not verify end to end.

No, but it becomes useful when several teams share one account and you must tell callers apart, cap usage and prove who did what.

Not as it stands. The repository says so itself: the authorizer denies everything by default and least privilege must be applied. It is a sample, with little activity on the repository when we read it.

The gateway is an AWS component, independent of the Dynatrace edition. The post mentions Dynatrace observability without distinguishing Managed from SaaS; check your edition’s documentation for how to ingest AWS logs.

Secure Amazon Bedrock access is proven by its logs: first put a real identity in the authorizer, cut the role’s permissions, then log the stage. The sample-ai-gateway-for-amazon-bedrock repository gives you the skeleton; the rest is your operating decision.

span.observer is an independent community blog, not affiliated with Dynatrace LLC. Dynatrace is a trademark of Dynatrace LLC; Amazon Bedrock is an Amazon Web Services service. Details change: check the official documentation.

#9681. AI Made Writing Code Cheap. Getting It Reviewed Now Takes 5x Longer, Says LinearB’s CEO

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

A developer using an AI assistant can open a pull request in minutes, yet the change still sits in a queue until a human reviewer picks it up. That is why agent-written pull requests wait 17.6 hours for a first review against 3.4 hours for human ones, even as enterprises spent $4.0 billion on AI coding tools in 2025, seven times the year before.

Today we sit down with Ori Keren, co-founder and CEO of LinearB, to discuss how the company grew from engineering dashboards into a context layer for agents, how it sells to boards that want proof of AI's return and where developer productivity goes once agents write much of the code.

Ishan Pandey: Welcome to Behind the Startup, Ori. Tell us about your journey and what made you build LinearB in the first place?

Ori Keren: Thanks for having me, Ishan. I started writing code as a kid, programming in BASIC on a Sinclair Spectrum in 1987, and I got my first developer job in 2000. From there I moved into management. I ran an engineering group at Interwise, which AT&T acquired, and then I was VP of R&D at CloudLock, which Cisco acquired in 2016. That's where I met Dan Lines, my co-founder.

What stayed with me from those years is how blind software development is. You run a team of a hundred engineers, and every week the business asks when something will ship or why it's late. You answer from gut feel and status meetings. Meanwhile, every answer is sitting in Git, in Jira and in your CI system, just never connected.

So in 2019, Dan and I started LinearB to connect it. We wanted to give engineering leaders real data on how their teams deliver, instead of gut feel, and then help them act on it. Helping teams act on the data is still what drives everything we build, and today those teams include agents.

Ishan Pandey: LinearB started in 2019 by giving engineering leaders delivery metrics, yet you have now rebuilt the platform around a knowledge graph of the whole software delivery lifecycle. What did you see in customer data over the past year that told you this called for a rebuild of the company's core?

Ori Keren: Two things, and they showed up in the data at the same time.

The first was that AI made writing code cheap but didn't make delivery faster. Our benchmarks cover 8.1 million pull requests from 4,800 teams. AI-assisted pull requests are about 2.6 times larger than unassisted ones. Pull requests opened by agents wait 17.6 hours for a first review, against 3.4 hours for human ones. The bottleneck simply moved downstream, into review, merge and ownership.

The second was why agents struggle. An agent starts every task cold. It has a good idea of the code, but it doesn't have the business context. It doesn't know that this service had two incidents last month, that this file has been rewritten five times this quarter, or who owns it. We had all of that, linked from ticket to release, for every customer.

That's when it clicked. Everyone else is focused on writing code. We hold a knowledge graph of everything happening across delivery, and that's exactly what agents and teams need. A dashboard can't hand that context to an agent, so we rebuilt LinearB around the graph itself. Context is the new king.

Ishan Pandey: When you raised your Series B in 2022, LinearB served more than 5,000 development teams. How has the customer base grown since then and which kind of company is now expanding fastest on the platform?

Ori Keren: We've moved up market. In 2022, a lot of our growth came bottom up, from engineering managers at fast-moving tech companies. Today our core is the enterprise, meaning organizations with hundreds or thousands of engineers, several AI coding tools running at once, and a board asking what it's getting for the spend. We're also seeing strong growth among healthcare organizations.

The pattern is consistent. A company adopts Copilot here, Cursor there and Claude Code somewhere else. Within a quarter or two, leadership realizes it can't answer basic questions, like whether the code holds up, where it's working and what it's costing. That's when they come to us, and that's when they expand.

Kraken is a good example of what that looks like. They used our MCP with an AI assistant to find out what was slowing their code reviews. It turned out to be time zones and reviewer availability, not change size. Within four months, they cut review time at the 90th percentile by more than half.

Ishan Pandey: Boards and CFOs now ask directly whether AI coding spend is paying off. How has that changed who signs a LinearB contract, from the VP of engineering to the CFO or CIO, along with how a deal is won?

Ori Keren: The SVP of engineering or CTO is still our executive buyer.

Who they answer to. Ken Ringdahl, the CTO at Emburse, puts our charts straight into his board decks because his board asks specifically about AI use and ROI. That's now normal.

There are a lot of company-wide AI initiatives now, driven by the CFO or CEO, and in the companies we work with, engineering is usually where AI spend is highest.

So finance is in the room far more often. Engineering leaders bring us in because they need numbers that hold up in front of a CFO, not a vanity metric from a vendor's own dashboard.

That changes how a deal is won. Five years ago, we won by showing a better cycle-time chart. Today we win by answering the finance question in the evaluation itself. We connect the data, and within days we show which teams are getting value from AI, which aren't, and what each delivered change costs. Token spend makes this sharper. In our 2026 AI benchmarks, which cover 253 engineering organizations, developers at the 90th percentile now spend $35.20 per coding day on tokens, up nearly 75% in three months. When a CFO sees that line, the conversation moves fast.

Ishan Pandey: LinearB built an audience through the Dev Interrupted podcast and free developer tools long before Gartner gave the category a Magic Quadrant. How does that community-led motion now work alongside enterprise sales and which channel brings in your largest customers today?

Ori Keren: Dev Interrupted was never meant as a lead generator. We started it because engineering leaders had nowhere to talk about the craft of running engineering. That trust turned out to be our moat. When a category gets a Magic Quadrant, every buyer suddenly has a shortlist. Our edge is that many of the people on the buying side have listened to the show for years, used our free tools, or borrowed our benchmarks for their own planning.

Today the two motions feed each other. Community and free tools create familiarity, often with a director or a staff engineer. Benchmarks and research give the champion something credible to take upstairs. Enterprise sales then turns that into an organization-wide rollout with security review, procurement and an ROI case.

Our largest deals close through our enterprise sales team, and when we trace them back, someone inside almost always knew LinearB before the first sales call. That's the compounding effect we're after.

Ishan Pandey: Your effort skill sends simple changes through cheaper agent runs while giving risky changes more care and more tokens. How do you price a product whose value is partly measured in tokens saved and what will the next skills for review and merge add for customers?

Ori Keren: First, a clarification. The effort skill isn't a cost-cutting tool that happens to touch quality. It's a judgment tool. It looks at a change's complexity and risk, using the full knowledge graph, and decides how hard the agent should work. Sometimes that means fewer tokens. On a fragile payments service, it means more, with careful, tested edits. The goal is the right effort on each change.

That's why we don't price on tokens saved. If we took a cut of savings, we'd be rewarded for making agents cheap rather than for making delivery better. Customers judge us on the cost of each delivered change, not the raw token bill.

The next skills go where the bottleneck now sits, in review and merge. They'll use the same context to help teams decide where human attention is needed and what can move faster. After that comes governance of AI-written code and spend optimization.

Ishan Pandey: Gartner sizes the developer productivity insight market at about $400 million while enterprises already spend billions on AI coding tools. How large can this category become once it measures and guides agents as well as people over the next three years?

Ori Keren: The $400 million figure describes the developer productivity insight category, platforms that give engineering leaders visibility into how their teams deliver software. We've always operated in that category, and we've also always gone beyond it. Our philosophy has been to explore, measure, act, and the act part now shows up in our agent skills.

Once a company spends that much on agents, a layer that decides how those agents should work, where they should spend effort and whether their output is safe to ship isn't a reporting tool anymore. It's part of the delivery system, like CI/CD or observability. So the right comparison isn't to other dashboards. It's a share of total spend on software delivery, human and agent combined.

What I'm confident about is the direction. We think it's time for the category to stop being something leaders look at once a month and become something agents consult on every change.

Ishan Pandey: For CTOs and VPs of engineering whose boards will ask them this year to prove AI's return, what is the first thing you would tell them to measure and which older metric should they stop reporting?

Ori Keren: Measure the cost per effective delivered change, not code generated, pull requests opened or lines accepted from an assistant. An effective change is one that merged, shipped and didn't come back as rework. Take what you spend on people and tokens, and divide it by those changes. You want effective changes trending up and the cost of each one trending down. That's the number that tells a board whether AI is paying off, and it holds up when finance pushes on it.

Emburse tracks exactly this. Over seven months, most of its code moved to AI, and its cost per effective pull request fell about 35%.

Right next to it, track what each model costs against the quality of the code it produces. The differences are bigger than most teams expect. Kraken found that two engineers can ship the same work while one burns thousands of dollars in tokens and the other spends hundreds, depending on which models they use and how.

Then stop reporting raw throughput, like pull requests or commits per developer, and above all, stop reporting AI adoption rates. Telling a board that 90% of your engineers use AI says nothing about return.

Inside engineering, though, keep measuring how work flows through your software factory. The bottlenecks haven't gone away. They've moved to review and release.

For CTOs and VPs of engineering heading into a board meeting, the practical takeaway is his metric. Cost per effective delivered change puts people and token spend over work that merged, shipped and stayed fixed, which gives a CFO a number to test. With AI coding spend compounding and the measurement category growing more than 40% a year, I expect the teams that adopt this kind of accounting early to have the easiest budget conversations of 2027. Leaders who want to compare their own teams can start with LinearB's free benchmarks report or the LinearB platform.

#9680. I Tried The Great British Bake Off’s Most Controversial Recipe—Here’s How It Went

The “technical challenge,” a blind-baking test where contestants receive the same recipe and ingredients, often with minimal or deliberately sparse instructions, is a staple of The Great British Bake Off. And contestants have seriously struggled with it over the years. But according to Paul Hollywood, this season’s challenge featuring blue cheese and roasted grape flatbreads was the worst yet. After 60 minutes of kneading, grape-roasting, and undercooking, the bakers produced trays of thick, raw flatbreads that Paul and Nigella could barely eat.

After bakers argued that an hour wasn’t enough, Paul said, “There’s plenty of time.” But fans, critics, and former bakers alike have been plenty vocal about their feelings. The popular opinion? The bakers were set up to fail—and also that the flavors seemed a little weird.

With all the controversy, I was curious to see if the challenge was even possible—so I tried it myself. While I purposefully did NOT watch the episode before my attempt, I did print the full recipe from the GBBO website. This recipe was definitely WAY more helpful than the one the bakers were given, and I followed it to the letter.

Here’s how it went: the good, the bad, and the very ugly.

The beginning? Very smooth. I put the grapes in the oven (the online recipe told me to roast them as a whole bunch rather than cutting them up) and made the bread dough, kneading it for the five minutes specified before letting it rest.

As soon as I set the dough aside to rest, I discovered how absolutely torturous technical downtime is. I was at an absolute loss. I had nothing to do…except read the recipe over and over again and make sure I knew what 8 cm and 23 cm looked like.

Interestingly enough, the bakers on the show didn’t have this downtime; they were busy cutting and roasting their grapes by then. That said, I don’t think that order was necessarily better; with the time spent slicing the grapes, they wouldn’t have had much time at ALL to roast—and not nearly enough to cool.

The grapes came out of the oven. They weren’t very roasted—as one of the bakers said, they just looked like “raw grapes”—but the recipe said 20 minutes and gave no indicators for how roasted they should be (and also I knew they needed to cool before stuffing), so I just went with it.

I dumped out the dough (a rude awakening after its 15-minute rest) and chopped it into eight pieces. Immediately, I realized I should have weighed the larger ball and divided it by eight so I could make sure all the pieces were equal, but I didn’t have much time to fuss, so I tried to make them roughly the same weight and moved on.

The recipe said to roll out each portion of dough into an 8 cm circle, fill it with five roasted grapes and one-eighth of the blue cheese, lift the edges of the circle up to pinch them together, then turn the little ball seam side down and roll the whole thing out into a 23 cm circle.

To begin, I cut my dough into wedges from the larger ball, and it was hard to roll them out into a circle to fill. But that was nothing compared to the problems I had rolling out the filled dough. First, the dough wasn’t rested enough, so it kept springing back at me as I tried to roll it out. But the bigger issue was the grapes. Since they were still pretty juicy, they started bursting as I rolled out the flatbread, flying to the edges and tearing holes in the dough as they oozed out.

After over 15 minutes of stuffing and rolling, my workstation was littered with burst grape guts. None of my flatbreads were 23 cm wide (I think the widest they got was 18?) and I still had three to roll out, but I also knew I needed to start cooking or I was going to have eight totally raw flatbreads at the end of time.

Cooking the flatbreads wasn’t a total disaster—I guess—but grape juice oozed out of the holes where they burst and left black patches of burnt sugar on the pan, which I had absolutely no time to clean out since I was still racing the clock. Fortunately, the flatbreads didn’t seem to need the full 90 seconds per side. In fact, they seemed to need constant attention to prevent them from burning, which was bad news since I was still trying to roll out the remaining three flatbreads on the side.

Time was up, and I had five cooked (burst) stuffed flatbreads on my sheet tray, three totally raw ones on the countertop, and a smoking pan. I now know how the bakers feel at the end of such challenges: slightly insane and utterly defeated.

Looking back on the challenge, I can honestly say that it was difficult and somewhat impossible. Ultimately, I couldn’t get all the flatbreads cooked in time, even though I was rolling them out much thinner than the bakers were. But while timing was definitely a problem, the bigger issue was the impossible stupidity of stuffing juicy grapes inside a flatbread and then trying to roll it out without the grapes bursting out and ruining the dough.

Since I managed to cook five flatbreads, I could (unlike Paul and Nigella) taste the finished result—but honestly, I wasn’t a fan. The blue cheese was WAY too strong, and the grapes felt like random pockets of juice in an otherwise savory flatbread. Overall, I wouldn’t recommend trying this challenge yourself—unless you want to be scrubbing the burnt bits of grape sugar off your pan for the next week.

#9679. Studying Abroad? How I Keep Up With Fast English Lectures Using Lecture Recording

My everyday English is fine. I can order food, argue about tabs vs spaces, and survive a group project. Then I started a CS master's in Toronto, and in week two my distributed systems professor said something like "so the follower just, you know, steps down if the term's stale" at full speed, and I wrote down "follower stairs down." Lecture recording, a transcript, and some patience got me out of that hole. Since then other international students keep asking me how I do it, so here are the answers in one place.

My first language is Mandarin. Everything below is from two semesters of trying things, including the ones that failed.

That's what I did first. It didn't work. If I didn't catch a sentence at full speed in the room, I usually didn't catch it the second time either, because my problem wasn't attention. It was parsing. Fast speech, swallowed syllables, and three new terms per sentence.

Reading fixes that. On a page, I can slow down, reread, and see where one word ends and the next begins. So the recording is just the raw material. The useful part is turning it into text.

Ask. Every time, every course. Most of my professors said yes for personal review. One said no for the discussion sections because classmates share unpublished research there, and I didn't record those. Some universities also have their own accessibility or recording policies, so check your course page too. I keep my recordings private and never post them.

For steps 3 to 5 I use the lecture recording page on AudioToText. You can record in the browser or upload an existing file, and after transcription you can translate the transcript into another language on the results page and export the original and the translation together. When signed in there are 240 free minutes per day, which covers a normal lecture day for me.

This is the one I feel strongest about: no.

If you only read the translation, you're studying the subject in your native language and still can't follow the next lecture in English. Exams, assignments, and office hours are all in English. What helped me was reading the English first, then using the translation only to check my understanding of the hard passages. Side by side, one paragraph at a time.

Also, translations of technical text can go wrong in a quiet way. "Commit" in a database lecture and "commit" in a Git context land on different Chinese words, and the translation doesn't always pick the right one. When the original and the translation disagree, I trust the English plus my notes.

First, before transcribing a lecture full of names and acronyms, I add those terms to a vocabulary group. It's an Advanced transcription feature and uses more credits per minute, so I only do it for the jargon-heavy weeks. In the other weeks, I let the standard transcript run and fix the odd term by hand, since the transcript is editable.

Second, I ask the AI to explain the term using the lecture itself. Something like: "In this lecture, what does the professor mean by 'stale term'? Explain it in simpler English." That last part matters. I ask for simpler English, not Chinese, because the goal is to understand the English explanation. Then I check the answer against the actual sentence in the transcript.

The terms go into a plain Markdown file in my course repo:

The "What the prof said" column is the important one. It's real English from a real expert, with the exact phrasing you'll hear again. After a few weeks, I noticed I could catch those phrases live.

Mostly good, not perfect. My professors' accents range from Scottish to Brazilian, and clear audio matters more than accent in my experience. The worst transcripts I got were from a back-row seat and from a seminar where three people talked at once. For seminars, turning on speaker identification helped a lot, because I could see who said what instead of one long block.

Accuracy also drops on specialized terms, which is why the vocabulary groups and the manual fixes exist. I treat every transcript as a draft that I'm allowed to correct.

Honest answer: the first three weeks felt like extra work. Recording, uploading, reading, glossary. About an hour per lecture.

By mid-semester, it dropped to around 30 minutes, mostly because I was getting lost less often in class. Fewer ??? marks meant less to fix later. My glossary file for distributed systems ended up with about 140 terms, and I read it on the subway before the final instead of rereading slides.

The bigger change was in office hours. I used to go in and say "I didn't understand lecture 5." Now I go in with a quote and a timestamp, and the professor answers in two minutes instead of re-teaching the whole thing.

If you're in your first semester abroad and feel like everyone else understands the joke you missed, you're not slow. You're decoding in real time while also learning the subject. Giving yourself a text version of the class to read afterwards is a reasonable fix for that.

Disclosure: I'm involved with AudioToText, the tool linked above. The workflow, the glossary, and the "follower stairs down" note are my own. This post was drafted with AI assistance and edited by me.

#9678. Classic Stuffing

While traditional stuffing is technically supposed to be stuffed inside the turkey to cook, that isn’t actually the ideal or even recommended way to cook your Thanksgiving turkey (or stuffing). I've found that you’ll achieve much better results by cooking them separately. By cooking your stuffing in a baking dish, you get crunchy, buttery pieces of bread on top and soft, bread pudding-esque pieces underneath. It's my perfect version of the holiday side—I tested it again and again, so it was worthy of your Thanksgiving table.

What People Are Saying:"[It's] an excellent recipe you can tweak it for taste. I like to up the onion by half again and use a lot more fresh sage." - GreenClover

"Using a [mandoline] made the final preparation fast and easy. It was a big hit over a lovely meal. The dressing brought high praise from two trained chefs." - RedFish

As I mentioned above, sourdough bread is my go-to for stuffing. The first step is to bake it! You'll need 2 sheets, or do this in batches. You want to dry it out, so bake for 15 to 20 minutes.

While that's toasting, it's time to cook the aromatics. Melt some butter, then cook the onions, leeks, and garlic until your kitchen smells amazing and everything is softened.

Time for the liquids: Simply whisk eggs, broth, milk, and some fresh herbs in a large measuring cup. You can use a touch of red pepper for a hint of spice, which I highly recommend, but if you have a spice-averse crowd, you can skip it.

When the bread is done toasting, turn the oven temp up to 375°. Prepare a 13" x 9" baking dish by coating it with a thin layer of butter.

Time to combine it all together: In a large bowl, mix the bread, aromatics, and liquid ingredients and toss until combined. You can let this sit at room temperature for up to 1 hour if you're planning ahead. Dot with even more butter, then bake until crispy. You can serve this stuffing warm or at room temperature.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.
