#9567. Add This Creamy Dip To Ground Beef For Juicier, More Flavorful Burgers

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The perfect burger can be hard to come by. When you're going out, Food Republic's list of the best burgers in every state can be helpful, and there are even some great fast food options. But when you're looking for a super juicy and flavorful homemade grilled or pan-fried patty, what's the best route to take?

Sometimes, it all comes down to what you mix into the ground beef. While Bobby Flay uses only salt and pepper to season his patties, some folks swear by Worcestershire sauce and garlic powder for a kick of flavor. But there's one ingredient you may not have thought of that will keep your end result wonderfully succulent. Try mixing some onion dip into your ground beef. It's one of the clever ingredients that make burgers juicier, and it will add loads of flavor.

Onion dips generally come seasoned with dried onion and garlic, salt, and other herbs, plus a little sugar for sweetness. Add to that the sour cream base, and you have a rich, bold, slightly tangy, umami-filled burst of flavor that won't overpower your taste buds. And because you're mixing the dip directly into the beef before cooking, it can help keep your patties nice and moist (as long as you don't overcook them). Sour cream is simply cultured cream, so it has a high moisture content, and the added seasonings aren't so coarse that they will burn before the beef itself is cooked.

When it comes to what dip to use, classics like Dean's French Onion or Daisy Sour Cream French Onion, which is available on Amazon, will work great, but pretty much any brand will work. Depending on how much tangy flavor you want, you'll need about a half-cup to a full cup of dip per 2 pounds of beef.

The beauty of using onion dip in your burgers is that it's a one-ingredient solution, but you can increase the intensity with extra onion powder or fresh minced or dried onions. Just don't overdo it on the onion pieces, or the patties could fall apart on the grill. If you're going heavy on the amount of dip you use, you may want to think about adding some breadcrumbs as a binding agent. Dried parsley makes a great mix-in, as do other Italian herbs, but you should start sparingly so they don't overpower the flavor you're aiming for.

As for toppings, the regular stuff will do, but you might want to hold off on the ketchup and mustard until you've had a bite. Caramelized onions are an obvious choice, or you can give your burger some crunch with crispy fried onions. And you can always add an extra dollop of onion dip on top for more creamy flavor and texture.

Lastly, this trick will also work with a dried dip mix. Just mix it in with sour cream before you make the burgers. And if you want a similarly juicy bite without the added zing, try using mayonnaise in your burger. But for a juicy texture and plenty of zesty flavor, grab that onion dip out of the fridge.

#9565. Who Makes Costco's Kirkland Signature Red Blend Wine?

Culinary mysteries span many topics, whether the origins of chicken à la king or the closely guarded composition of Coca-Cola. Yet one unknown that perpetually probes consumers is which producer is behind Costco's private-label alcohol. The Kirkland Signature labels conceal a treasure trove of well-priced bottles, spanning not only every major liquor style, but also a varied selection of wine and (formerly) beer.

A bottle label that commands special intrigue is the Kirkland Signature California Red Blend. This vino comes packaged in an eye-catching 1.5-liter bottle, all while sold for under $10. You'd think that such a size would make sleuthing the producer tricky. However, the brand behind this budget pick is listed directly on the bottle: DC Flynt MW Selections.  A large company responsible for both cellaring and bottling, this producer and distributor oversees a widespread U.S. and global portfolio, making it a natural match for Costco.

DC Flynt MW Selections is primarily headquartered in Louisiana, but the Kirkland Signature bottle lists the origin as Modesto, California. This suggests that at least some of the grapes are assembled in California's Central Valley region, as Modesto is only about two hours from Napa Valley — although precise vineyard sourcing is unknown. The same brand is also behind bottles from Sonoma, Napa, and Alexander Valley. Similarly, it produces Kirkland Signature's chardonnay as well.

As one of the least expensive Kirkland Signature wines, you might not expect an oenophile-appreciated experience with this bottle. Yet despite this accessible price point, the wine garners positive reviews: "A proof that [mass-marketed] wines can actually be good," noted Vivino reviewer Anton A., who gave the wine 4 stars. On the platform, the wine is rated 3.7 out of 5 stars, with over 3,500 reviews. Furthermore, other reviewers have given it favorable scores, praising the wine's balance of fruit-forward and spice flavors.

Typically, affordable California red blends are known for sweet "jammy" flavors, meaning the composition is heavy on sugar. Yet as noted right on the Kirkland label itself, this bottling strays from aggressive fruit-forwardness. Notes of oak and spice help contrast the fruit, a sentiment upheld by reviewers: "More [Bordeaux-like] than a California fruit bomb, but extremely tasty," noted another Vivino user — although some drinkers do take issue with its moderate palate. "[Not] flavorful enough, not jammy enough, not [oaky] enough," critiqued a Reddit user. Still, at a price point that even beats out affordable Trader Joe's picks, it's wine worth adding to a Costco shopping haul.

#9564. The Key To The Perfect Pie Crust Is In These 5 Simple Rules

Admit it, a pie is only as good as its crust. No matter how good the filling is, a flaky, buttery crust is what separates the good from the great. But how to achieve the pie crust of your (and your guests’) dreams? The master of all things baking, Senior Food Editor Makinze Gore, is here to explain her five golden rules of pie crust—just in time for the holidays.

A buttery, flaky pie crust is the stuff of dreams; to achieve this, Gore says it’s essential to use cold butter. The same goes for many flaky pastries and baked goods, as the steam that cold butter releases as it melts creates those layers inside the crust. If you use butter that isn’t cold, it will melt too quickly—it can even melt just during the process of rolling the dough out if it's warm enough, which won’t produce any steam. Warm butter will leave you with a dense, mealy crust.

The size of your butter chunks will affect the end product. Gore says larger and smaller chunks can both work, but larger chunks leave a flakier crust, while smaller chunks let the crust hold more intricate designs. Typically, you want your chunks to be at least pea-sized to form the steam pockets required to create flaky layers.

Sensing a theme here? Gore says it’s vitally important to chill your dough at several points throughout the process. This is because you need to keep the butter cold, as it will warm up as you work with it. Gore recommends chilling your crust after you first make it, after rolling it out, before crimping it, and once more before baking it. This will help keep the butter cold and prevent the crust from shrinking as it bakes.

One great trick to ensure an even bake is to use a metal pie tin. Metal conducts heat better than glass, so it bakes the crust more evenly, though glass does have some benefits. Baking pie crust in a glass pie dish lets you see the bottom of the crust and know exactly when it’s perfectly cooked.

Another tip Gore says will help bake your crust more evenly is to set a baking sheet in the oven as it preheats, then to place the pie tin on top of the hot baking sheet as it cooks. This extra heat helps the crust cook slightly faster, giving it more time to set before the liquid filling seeps in.

#9563. The Everyday Nutrient Linked To 32% Lower Dementia Risk

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Moderate intake of choline, a nutrient found in eggs, fish and legumes, is linked to a lower risk of dementia.

Older adults consuming moderately high amounts had a 32 percent lower dementia risk than those consuming the least.

However, the highest intake was not associated with a clear benefit, suggesting that more is not necessarily better.

The research followed over 5,000 American adults, whose average age was almost 69, for around eight years.

Participants were initially free of dementia but around 500 developed the condition during follow-up.

After dividing participants into five groups according to choline intake, the researchers found a 32 percent lower dementia risk in the second-highest group than in the lowest, after accounting for other factors.

However, there was no statistically clear reduction in the highest-intake group.

The result therefore points towards a potentially beneficial range, rather than a steady fall in risk with every increase in consumption.

The researchers then combined their results with four previous studies to assess the broader pattern.

Together, these followed almost 138,000 people and recorded around 2,500 cases of dementia.

In the combined analysis, dementia risk fell as choline intake rose to approximately 465 milligrams per day, with no further reduction beyond that level.

Choline helps the brain produce acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in learning and memory.

It also supplies building blocks for the membranes surrounding brain cells, helping maintain their structure and communication.

These roles could help explain a link between choline and cognitive ageing, although they do not prove that consuming more prevents dementia.

The nutrient also participates in processes that regulate homocysteine, a substance linked to problems with blood vessels and cognitive function.

Eggs, meat, poultry and nuts were among the main sources of choline in the American participants’ diets.

People consuming more choline obtained a greater proportion of it from eggs.

Crucially, the analysis assessed choline from food and did not include intake from supplements.

The findings therefore cannot establish whether choline supplements would lower dementia risk.

The study was published in the Nutrition Journal (Chen et al., 2026).

#9562. The best Thanksgiving baking tips from Ina Garten, Erin McDowell, and more pro bakers: Top tips from the Things Bakers Know podcast.

It’s the most wonderful baking season of the year, and to help you bake your best, we have top tips from some of the country’s best bakers, pulled from conversations on the Things Bakers Know podcast. Below, you’ll find Thanksgiving strategies from upcoming podcast guests Ina Garten (episode dropping November 23!) and King Arthur’s Martin Philip (find his episode November 16), as well as guests from previously aired episodes, including Erin McDowell, Helen Goh, and many more of our baking friends.

“The one thing I think people think they can do is multiply a recipe times four and think it’s going to come out fine, which it won’t,” Ina shared on her forthcoming podcast episode. Instead of taking one recipe and just multiplying by three or four, she suggests either baking the original recipe multiple times, or doubling it and baking two or three times, depending on how many people you’re feeding. Just don’t multiply more than once! If you do, the leavening and flavoring starts to get thrown off.

If you’re baking for a lot of people, Ina also suggests making recipes scaled for a baking sheet. As she explains, “It’s easier to bake, and it’s easier to cut.” We’d recommend Slab Chocolate Pecan Pie, Pumpkin Cake Bars with Cream Cheese Frosting, or Walnut and Oat Slab Pie.

While you may be excited to try out a show-stopping recipe from a brand-new cookbook, Ina recommends resisting temptation. “You don’t want to test something you haven’t made a million times,” she cautions. “Even for me, it adds enormous stress.” Instead of turning to a first-time recipe, Ina highly recommends that you “do the things you know will come out perfectly every time.” And if you do want to make a new-to-you recipe this Thanksgiving, consider baking it once or twice in the weeks leading up to the holiday, so you have the chance to practice and work out any kinks (like figuring out make-ahead components or fridge storage) before hosting on the big day.

No one wants a soggy bottom on their pie, especially a super-juicy one like apple pie. Erin McDowell has lots of tips to avoid a soggy bottom, but her biggest one is to precook your apple filling before assembling your pie. “We can't necessarily predict how juicy any given fruit is, so even if you're using the same apple … each time, they are going to be a little bit different,” she explained on our podcast episode all about apples. Precooking the filling allows you to adjust based on the juiciness of the fruit you’re using that day. “If you're dealing with not-very-juicy apples, you may not have to cook it as long. If they're really juicy, you may have to cook it longer, but the process is the same.”

Pie crust can be incredibly intimidating for some bakers. But pie queen Stacey Mei Yan Fong says the key to success is sometimes to chill out, figuratively and literally. “The best thing you can do is just chill, as in calm down. You're not doing brain surgery,” she reminded Jessica in our Thanksgiving pie episode. “And also use your fridge!” As she points out, “the minute things start getting too wet or things start getting too warm, that's when people panic.” So take a moment to chill the dough and make it easier to work with. If the butter's getting soft or your pie dough is getting difficult to work with, just put it in the fridge to cool down for 10 to 15 minutes.

It’s not just the fridge, either — your freezer can also be incredibly helpful. Stacey likes to freeze her pies before baking, which she says helps the crimping hold its shape as it bakes. And remember that, as Stacey points out, “Pie is kind of a lesson in patience.”

On our special Holiday Q+A Extravaganza dropping November 23, King Arthur’s Director of Baking Education Amber Eisler has a crucial tip for avoiding runny apple pies — make sure you see your pie filling actively bubbling through the vents in your pie crust. As she explains, “It means the filling has boiled and bubbled, so the starches in the filling are actually thickening, which is a super important part of [avoiding a soupy pie].”

There’s a lot of cooking and baking happening around Thanksgiving, which means your oven can get pretty crowded, pretty quickly. But be wary of overfilling it. Even though your oven may have up to three racks inside, Martin Philips cautions against using them all at the same time. “Don’t make the mistake of crowding the oven when it comes to rolls. Let bread have its moment,” he says. Bake your pies the day before to save oven space; a turkey, too will stay hot out of the oven for hours. When baking rolls, you want “top and bottom heat, use your convection setting, make sure that air is moving,” says Martin. “Guard the rolls, y’all!”

Cookbook author and professional psychologist Helen Goh believes in the power of baking to bring meaning and fulfillment to our lives. During this busy holiday season, full of messy kitchens, family squabbles, lengthy to-do lists, and lots of hosting, it can be easy to get overwhelmed. But baking can actually be a calming, comforting activity right now. “Some people say baking makes them nervous because you have to focus,” says Helen. But part of the therapeutic effect of baking comes from forcing us to focus on a single task at hand. As she points out, “that takes you away from all that white noise about what you did yesterday or what's going to happen tomorrow,” and instead allows you to live mindfully in the moment.

Happy Thanksgiving from all of us here at King Arthur. If you run into baking troubles or just need a little support in the kitchen, our Baker’s Hotline is here to help.

#9561. Forget Mayo: Add This Creamy Ingredient To Tuna Salad (Hint: It's Egg Free)

Finding a delicious substitute for mayo in tuna salad can be a challenge, especially if you're looking for an egg-free alternative that's still creamy. But if you like a bit of garlic in yours, then toum — a Lebanese spread as rich in flavor as it is in fluffiness — is the answer you've been looking for.

Toum is a bit unique in that it relies on hefty amounts of garlic, oil, and vigorous blending to emulsify. Far lighter in texture than mayonnaise but not quite as airy as whipped cream, it's a perfect middle ground that imparts serious flavor to fish. While it won't have quite the same richness as mayonnaise, since it lacks eggs, this can actually work in your favor. It gives your final product a lighter flavor profile that's highly conducive to other simple ways to level up tuna salad, such as adding horseradish or capers. It's perfect for when you want a protein-laden lunch that doesn't feel too heavy and won't leave you in need of a nap.

Served cold, it's delicious. But when served warm in a tuna melt, the heat brings out the aromas of garlic in a way that's beyond anything else. The pungent notes fill your nostrils and blend with cheeses and toasted bread to create something as satisfying as any cheeseburger. Just be careful not to let any fall out, as toum's oil-based emulsion can separate or scorch when exposed to excessive heat.

If you like a denser tuna salad, one packed with hearty chunks and thick vegetables, then mixing in a dollop of toum and calling it a day works just fine. However, if you want something quite light and creamy, almost like a tonnato sauce, then you need some high-powered beating action. By adding the toum and tuna to a stand mixer or a bowl with an electric hand mixer, you shred the fish into fine pieces. This allows the fluffy nature of the garlic spread to almost suspend the protein, giving the illusion of increased volume without actually adding any additional ingredients.

Toum can be quite acidic depending on the brand and recipe, and the lemon juice can quickly work with any pickles or relish to make your tuna salad a bit overpowering. To avoid anything too intense, you may want to switch to sweeter varieties. Still, if you're a diehard believer in acidic additions, apples, hot honey (a true kitchen multitasker), or a pinch of sugar can all help balance acidity quite well and add little nuances of their own that work well with garlic.

#9557. What It Means When You Hear A Cowbell Ring At McDonald's

McDonald's is one of the biggest chains in the world, so being curious about what goes on behind the scenes is only natural. People love to throw around wild theories (no, the chicken nuggets aren't made from pink slime), but there are plenty of factual goings-on that might surprise fans. For instance, many customers are shocked to learn that McDonald's cooks aren't flipping your patties, or that every time you order a Quarter Pounder, you're setting off a cowbell in the kitchen.

To get to the bottom of this, Food Republic reached out to sisters Melissa Montes Blanco and Kristina Montes, third-generation owners and operators of several McDonald's locations. According to them, the cowbell rings because the Quarter Pounder is cooked to order. "When you go through the [drive-thru] or [order] delivery, whenever the order comes in, we will hear a cowbell in the kitchen, and that signals to the team to drop the meat at that point," they explained.

As of writing, the Quarter Pounder is McDonald's only burger made with fresh, never-frozen beef. When preparing meat for the Big Mac or cheeseburger, the frozen patties are batch-cooked and left in heated holding cabinets, so they can be assembled in seconds. The Quarter Pounder is a slightly more involved process, so when a customer places an order, the crew needs to be ready to throw a patty on the grill. It doesn't help that the patty takes much longer to cook. According to McDonald's, a regular patty takes around 42 seconds on the grill, while a Quarter Pounder patty nearly triples that at 112 seconds (almost two minutes). Fast food is in the name, so speed is everything, and a cowbell is a pretty effective way to spring the crew into action. The Montes sisters went on to explain that this extra time may be why you're sometimes asked to pull forward and wait outside of the drive-thru queue.

McDonald's has the inner workings of the fast food game down to a science, from sensors that alert employees when a car pulls into the drive-thru to smart weight-checking scales for delivery orders that compare the total weight of the bag against expected targets to flag missing items before it leaves the kitchen. Most of its stores operated like a well-oiled machine long before the fresh-beef Quarter Pounder was introduced in 2018, so are the cowbells really necessary? According to several employees, they're nothing more than a nuisance.

The alarm is part of McDonald's Kitchen Video System (KVS), which functions as a replacement for paper tickets by showing orders on screen for the crew. Alerts have traditionally been beeps and buzzes, so employees were caught off guard when a cowbell joined the mix. After the new grill display was installed, one self-identified employee took to Reddit to share their candid thoughts, claiming that "[it was] driving virtually everyone bats." They added, "It plays [an] unbelievably grating and repetitive cowbell sample instead of something more to the point ... It's annoying as hell[,] and nobody likes it except for a single manager. I thought about doing everyone a favor and just unplugging the speakers." A quick scroll through the replies was enough to show that this employee was far from alone, with plenty of coworkers piling on to share their own cowbell horror stories.

Despite waves of employee complaints, the cowbells don't seem to be going anywhere. McDonald's hasn't publicly responded to the backlash, and a November 2026 TikTok from McDonald's franchisee and content creator McBossladi has those all-too-familiar cowbells ringing in the background.

#9556. Pumpkin Chiffon Pie

Classic pumpkin pie may be the most well-known pumpkin pie come the holidays, but let us make our case for its underappreciated, fancy cousin: Pumpkin Chiffon Pie. Impossibly light and fluffy, the filling is made by folding meringue into a pumpkin curd-esque mixture for a slice that truly is light as a feather. With this at your Thanksgiving table, we doubt anyone would miss the classic.

What People Are Saying:“Best Pumpkin Chiffon! I have tried multiple recipes and this one was easy and delicious! My husband loved it! Thanks so much! Merry Christmas!” - PurpleWheel

Before making the filling, we need to make and bake our pie crust. Start by preheating the oven to 375° and lightly greasing a 9” pie dish with cooking spray.

On a clean, lightly floured surface, roll out your pie dough into a 12” circle of even thickness. Carefully drape it over the prepared pie dish and gently press it into the bottom and edges, taking care not to stretch the dough and create weak points. Prick the bottom of the dough with a fork to prevent bubbling while baking, then trim any excess dough from the edges so you have about 1” of overhang. Tuck the overhang under itself and crimp the edges. Then, place the dough into the fridge to chill for 30 minutes (or, if you’re in a rush, into the freezer for 10 minutes).

Remove the chilled crust from the refrigerator and line it with parchment paper. Fill the pie dish with dried beans or pie weights and place it into the oven to blind bake for about 18 to 20 minutes. Once the edges are lightly golden, remove the parchment and weights and bake for 5 to 10 minutes more, until fully golden and cooked through. Remove the crust from the oven and place it in the fridge to cool for at least 2 hours.

Once the crust has chilled completely, place a medium saucepan on the stove and whisk together ½ cup sugar with the gelatin, pumpkin pie spice, and salt.

Then, in a medium bowl, whisk together the pumpkin puree, egg yolks, and milk until smooth, then pour the mixture into the saucepan with the sugar and gelatin mixture and whisk to combine.

Turn the burner under the saucepan on to medium heat and stir constantly until the mixture is hot and small bubbles are beginning to form around the edges. Remove the saucepan from the heat and transfer the mixture to a large bowl to cool to room temperature.

In a separate bowl, use a hand mixer to beat together the egg whites and cream of tartar until soft peaks form. Then, add the remaining ¼ cup sugar, one tablespoon at a time, continuing to beat until stiff peaks form.

Transfer ¼ of the whipped egg whites into the cooled pumpkin mixture and gently fold to combine. Then add the remaining egg whites and fold to combine again. Pour the mixture into the cooled pie crust and smooth the top before placing it into the refrigerator for at least 4 hours and up to overnight. Once it has cooled and set completely, top the pie with whipped cream and a sprinkle of pumpkin spice before slicing and serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found below.

A chiffon is typically made with a filling (often containing gelatin, like in this recipe) that's usually cooked over a double boiler before whipped cream gets folded in for a luxurious texture. The whole thing is poured into a pre-baked (like in this recipe) or no-bake crust and refrigerated.

If you want to save time (and counter space) by making your Thanksgiving dishes ahead of time, this is the pie for you. The entire pie requires chilling for at least four hours, up to overnight before serving, so you can easily make this the day before, then simply top with whipped cream when you're ready to serve. Leftovers can be stored covered in the refrigerator for up to 3 days.

#9555. Two Personality Traits Linked To A Sharper Mind

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

Intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of beauty are both linked to stronger thinking skills.

People with these qualities tend to perform better on tests of literacy, numeracy and problem-solving.

The findings suggest that a person’s interest in ideas and aesthetic experiences may offer clues to their cognitive abilities.

Curiosity could encourage people to seek out opportunities to learn, while stronger thinking skills could make exploring complex ideas more rewarding, with both processes reinforcing one another.

Intellectual curiosity involves enjoying ideas, wanting to understand things and being drawn to questions that require thought.

Aesthetic sensitivity describes an appreciation of art and beauty.

Both qualities belong to the broader personality trait of openness to experience, which captures how receptive people are to unfamiliar ideas and experiences.

However, openness also includes creative imagination, and this aspect showed no significant independent association with cognitive performance.

Imagination, curiosity and an appreciation of beauty may overlap in everyday life, but their relationships with thinking skills differ.

The conclusions come from an analysis of almost 68,000 people across 12 countries, including Canada, Germany, Italy and New Zealand.

They completed personality questionnaires alongside assessments of literacy, numeracy and the ability to solve problems as circumstances change.

Intellectual curiosity and aesthetic sensitivity were linked to better performance across all three assessments, even after accounting for other personality traits.

The connections between personality and cognitive skills also varied between countries.

Educational systems and cultural practices could help explain such differences, although the reasons remain uncertain.

Overall, the findings link both a desire to understand the world and an appreciation of its beauty with stronger thinking skills.

The study was published in the journal Large-scale Assessments in Education (Rammstedt et al., 2026).

#9554. How to turn any bread dough into rolls: Transform your favorite bread loaf into shareable rolls.

So you have a beloved bread recipe that you'd like to turn into fluffy, single-serving rolls, but you don’t know where to start. We’re here to help — let’s get rolling!

Rolls are basically just tiny bread. Which means that, yes, you can technically make a pan of rolls out of any bread dough.

But first, consider the recipe and what type of rolls you're looking to make. If you want soft, fluffy pull-apart rolls (typically baked nestled together in a pan), consider starting with an enriched dough like brioche, milk bread, or challah. If you want crusty, European-style rolls (often baked on sheet trays), start with a leaner dough, such as this pain au levain.

Essentially, the type of bread you start with will determine the type of rolls you make, so plan accordingly.

Turning a bread recipe into rolls is simple: After the dough has had its first rise (otherwise known as its bulk ferment), divide it into small pieces, shape them into rolls, give them a final rise, and bake. The good news is that you don’t need to make any changes to the recipe itself — simply prepare the dough as written and leave it to undergo its first rise.

Once the bread dough has risen, it's time to divide it. Consider: How many rolls do you want, and how large do you want them to be?

Your best bet for even-sized rolls is to grab a calculator and kitchen scale. While you could divide your dough by eye, it’s faster, easier, and more accurate to use the weight measurements, if possible.

For size reference, the pre-bake weight of dinner rolls typically falls between 60g to 80g each. Imagine a 60g roll as the size of a plum when baked, while a baked 80g roll is closer to a Granny Smith apple. Moving up in the ranks are burger buns, which weigh around 100g or so pre-bake.

Here's how much each rolls should weigh before baking:

If you want small-to-medium dinner rolls: 60g to 70g

If you want medium-to-large dinner rolls: 80g to 90g

If you want extra-large dinner rolls or burger buns: 100g to 110g

Let’s say you’re using our Back-of-the-Bag Oatmeal Bread recipe. The total weight of the dough is about 830g. If your first thought is, “I want eight rolls!” you’re going to wind up with eight oat-y burger bun-sized rolls, because 830g divided by eight is just over 100g per roll. That's likely too large if you're looking to make standard dinner rolls.

To ensure you get properly sized rolls, it’s easiest to start by dividing the total weight of the dough by the weight of the size you want your rolls to be, rather than the number of rolls you want. In this case, 830g ÷ 75g = 11 large dinner rolls.

Once divided, it's time to shape the pieces of bread dough. If you’ve never shaped dinner rolls, have no fear! We have you covered, no matter the shape you choose. Basic round rolls? Got it. Fancy shapes? Yep. Braided rolls? You bet. And so much more. Often it helps to see the process in action, especially when it comes to hand positioning when shaping rolls.

For gluten-free breads, scoop the “dough” into a greased muffin pan rather than attempt to shape rolls by hand, since the dough is more like batter. If you're making medium or large gluten-free rolls, check out our Gluten-Free Dinner Rolls recipe for more details.

Small rolls won’t take as long to bake as a loaf would. Most will take around 20 to 30 minutes to bake, depending on their size. You can usually stick with the temperature your original recipe calls for, but 350°F is a safe bet, too.

A final note: Rolls baked close together in "pull-apart" style will usually take a bit longer to bake than they would if they were spaced out on a baking sheet.

And remember, if you make more rolls than you can eat in one sitting, you can always freeze and bake them.

We're diving deep on rolls ahead of Thanksgiving in our latest podcast episode, all about rolls.

#9549. I’m A Professional Cook & My Secret To Perfectly Smooth Gravy Is This $4 Pantry Staple

Gravy is one of the most problematic dishes on the Thanksgiving table. Every year, home cooks struggle and sweat over gravy that’s too thin, too greasy, or—worst of all—lumpy. All while your relatives watch and the turkey gets cold.

Making the gravy the day before is a surefire way to avoid the last-minute panic. But on holidays when prepping ahead just isn’t in the cards, one simple hack can solve your gravy woes: a $4 pantry staple that will thicken up any gravy in mere minutes—without any lumps.

The secret to perfectly smooth gravy is Wondra flour. Known to chefs and home cooks alike for its bright blue cylindrical can, Wondra is wheat flour that has been pre-gelatinized, dried, and finely milled so it dissolves more easily and thickens sauces faster than regular flour. This means you can whisk it directly into any gravy (no matter the temperature!) without worry about clumping—and it will thicken that gravy almost immediately.

If you’re making gravy from scratch with no other thickener besides Wondra, I recommend starting with 1 tablespoon for every cup of stock and/or drippings. You can do this by heating the drippings or stock in a pot on the stove, then just whisking in the Wondra. It should thicken within a few minutes. If your drippings don’t have a ton of fat, I recommend whisking in a little butter too, to help with the flavor.

If you’re using Wondra to troubleshoot a gravy that’s too thin, I recommend whisking in a few teaspoons at a time. The Wondra should do its thickening magic within a minute or two after it goes in, and then you can decide whether you need more.

While Wondra flour is great for thickening gravies and sauces, it’s far from a one-trick pony. I’ve used it to coat white fish (such as tilapia) before pan-searing to give it a beautifully thin, crispy crust—and help prevent the fish from sticking to the pan. It’s also a common ingredient in batters for fried foods, since its lower protein content helps form a lighter, crispier crust—and it’s also a magical way to get a flakier pastry dough. So even if you only make gravy once a year, that blue canister won’t go to waste.

#9538. Speaking Faster Can Make You More Persuasive — Until This Happens

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Speaking at a lively pace can make a strong argument more convincing, but rushing can weaken its impact.

Very fast speech makes it harder for listeners to weigh up what they hear, reducing the advantage that good reasons have over weak ones.

The findings suggest that persuading someone depends partly on giving them enough opportunity to think.

The conclusions come from six experiments involving almost 4,000 people who listened to persuasive messages delivered at different speeds.

Across the experiments, increasing the pace from very slow speech initially improved impressions of the speaker’s confidence and encouraged closer consideration of the message.

However, these benefits eventually weakened or reversed as the delivery became faster.

This helps explain why simply telling someone to speak more quickly is incomplete advice.

A faster delivery can make an argument easier to engage with until the listener begins struggling to keep up.

Crucially, the consequences depend on whether the reasons being offered stand up to scrutiny.

In the two main experiments, listeners heard a proposal that would allow university students to pay lower tuition fees in exchange for working part-time.

Some heard strong arguments emphasising benefits such as smaller classes and better services.

Others heard weak arguments that included reduced leisure time and superficial improvements to the campus.

The recordings were digitally altered to change speaking speed while keeping other vocal features, such as pitch and intonation, unchanged.

Participants then rated their support for the proposal, with some also recording the thoughts that had occurred to them while listening.

The combined results showed that strong arguments gained an increasing advantage over weak ones as speech became faster, but lost some of that advantage at higher speeds.

In other words, delivery affected how effectively listeners distinguished a convincing case from an unconvincing one.

A central part of persuasion is how carefully people consider the reasons they are given.

When listeners examine a message closely, they have more opportunity to recognise its strengths, spot its weaknesses and form their own reactions.

This benefits a strong argument, while exposing the shortcomings of a weak one.

Very fast delivery can interfere with that process, making the merits of the message less influential.

The analyses suggested that changes in how easily listeners felt they could follow the reasoning helped explain this pattern.

Although speaking speed also affected how confident the speaker sounded, confidence alone did not adequately explain the overall pattern.

One possible reason very slow speech is less effective is that it makes sustaining attention more demanding, while excessively fast speech leaves too little time to absorb the content.

The experiments tested seven speaking speeds, ranging from 113 to 218 words per minute, but did not establish one ideal pace.

The most effective delivery is likely to depend on factors including the complexity of the message, the audience and the presence of distractions.

The findings also concern recorded persuasive messages, so they do not establish a universal rule for every conversation or public speech.

For someone presenting a strong case, the findings suggest keeping the delivery lively while giving listeners time to follow the reasoning.

Rushing may reduce the very scrutiny that would otherwise make a good argument convincing.

The study was published in the Journal of Nonverbal Behavior (Guyer et al., 2025).

#9534. Pecan Pie Brownies

Making Thanksgiving dinner is already a Herculean task, but adding dessert to your list of responsibilities can feel like almost too much. This pecan pie makes things easy, giving you the perfect sweet treat to serve after a long, filling dinner without adding too much extra work. This seasonal twist on brownies skips the pie crust and combines two classic desserts in one delicious bite. The syrupy pecan pie topping seeps into the brownies, making them rich, flavorful, and just the right amount of moist.

The best part? These brownies are the perfect make-ahead dessert for your holiday party. Make them the day before the party, pop them (tightly wrapped or in an airtight container!) into the fridge, and forget about them until ready to serve.

Start by preheating your oven to 325°F. Grab a 9"x9" baking pan, grease it with cooking spray, and line it with parchment paper. Next, make the brownie batter following the directions on the box. Pour it into the pan and bake until the brownies are just a little underdone—poke the center with a tester, and if you see a few moist crumbs, they’re ready (this should take about 20 minutes). While the brownies are baking, grab a medium bowl and whisk together the corn syrup, brown sugar, butter, molasses, vanilla, and salt until nice and smooth. Add the eggs and whisk until everything’s well combined. Then, stir in the pecans so they’re all coated in the mixture.

Once the brownies are out of the oven, bump up the temperature to 350°F. Spoon the pecan mixture over the brownies and spread it out evenly. Pop the pan back in the oven and bake for another 40 to 45 minutes, or until the pecan topping feels springy and has thickened up.

Let the brownies cool down to room temperature first, then pop them in the fridge for about an hour until they’re cold and set.

If you’d like, finish them off with a drizzle of caramel sauce before serving.

#9531. Aggressive Policing as a Public Health Issue

The medical field has paid increased attention to the negative health impacts of systemic racism, discrimination, poverty, and other societal forces that are known to cause poorer health. This includes awareness of the need to assess and address racial and other health disparities and focus on principles of diversity, equity, and inclusion. We have moved beyond the framing of these issues as moral imperatives to understanding how they are related to individual and public health.

Discussion of the health harms of aggressive policing has also increased over the last 2 years, spurred by the frequent and well-publicized deaths of Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC). What has been viewed as a political issue is now understood as a public health/health inequity concern. Two articles that have helped change the way the medical community views these issues were published in 2021:

Both of these pieces help illustrate the ongoing shift in how police violence and aggressive policing have specific and disproportionate impacts on communities of color.

The first article makes several key points in its assertion that policing concerns should be viewed as health issues. It begins with this statement:

“Marginalized communities have a long history of naming the systemic racism and harms of police violence to health and well-being and recognizing their roots in the oppression of Black and Indigenous communities.”

The article cites data indicating that BIPOC are far more likely to be killed by police than White Americans, noting that death at the hands of a police officer is the sixth leading cause of death for young Black men. Similarly, Black and Indigenous women are more likely to be killed by a police officer than their White counterparts.

The second article also looks at specific data related to the disparate impact of what is describes as the “overexposure” to aggressive policing strategies among Black communities, serving to increase already existing health disparities in such communities. The article authors noted:

“Indeed, aggressive policing strategies employed by law enforcement agencies across the country have been hypothesized to degrade health and well-being, even among people who themselves have not experienced contact with police. Perhaps even more important, aggressive policing is thought to contribute to significant population health inequities, as these practices are concentrated on — and thus exacerbate — the health challenges faced by racialized populations.”

The authors of the article cited data from an organization called Campaign Zero.3 This group’s website includes data that also helps demonstrated the negative impact of aggressive policing, or what they describe as “broken windows” policing. This form of policing has led to the overpolicing of communities of color with resulting excessive force, leading to unnecessary deaths.

“Meanwhile, the vast majority of arrests are for low-level, nonviolent activities in encounters that often escalate to deadly force. For example, in 2014, police killed at least 287 people who were involved in minor offenses and harmless activities like sleeping in parks, possessing drugs, looking “suspicious” or having a mental health crisis. These activities are often symptoms of underlying issues of drug addiction, homelessness, and mental illness, which should be treated by health care professionals and social workers rather than the police.”

These 3 examples of the evolving understanding of how to view police aggressiveness highlight the need for future research and data collection. They also highlight the need for PAs, nurse practitioners, and other medical providers to assess the health impact of high-impact policing on their patients and to advocate for changes to a policing system that results in furthering existing health disparities.

1. Fleming PJ, Lopez WD, Spolum M, Anderson RE, Reyes AG, Schulz AJ. Policing is a public health issue: the important role of health educators. Health Educ Behav. 2021:10901981211001010. doi:10.1177/10901981211001010

2. Esposito M, Larimore S, Lee H. Aggressive policing, health, and health equity. Health Policy Brief. Health Affairs. April 30, 2021. doi:10.1377/hpb20210412.997570.

3. Campaign Zero. https://www.joincampaignzero.org/solutions#solutionsoverview

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.

#9527. Glace Drops At-Home Version Of Its Viral Hot Chocolate

All the chocolate, none of the NYC lines.

If you've spent any time on food TikTok, you've probably come across Glace's famous S'mores Hot Chocolate. The New York City dessert shop has become a social media sensation thanks to its ridiculously rich hot chocolate, complete with a thick ring of toasted marshmallow fluff around the cup and hefty scoop of whipped cream to top it off. And now you won't have to book a trip to Manhattan and stand in line just to try it.

Glace has officially launched its first-ever at-home hot chocolate mix, giving fans across the country the opportunity to recreate its signature drink without leaving their kitchens. And given how popular the in-store sensation has become, I'm guessing plenty of people will add this easy-to-duplicate version to their holiday wish lists.

Founded by Sasha Zabar in 2023, Glace first opened on New York City's Upper East Side, where its over-the-top S'mores Hot Chocolate quickly became the star of the menu. The drink, which features rich drinking chocolate surrounded by a toasted marshmallow rim, has attracted plenty of attention online.

Since then, the brand has continued to dominate social media with other over-the-top menu items like its à la mode Warm Brownie Pudding Cake and Matcha Fudge Sundae, and has also expanded with a seasonal holiday truck at Rockefeller Center and Glace Candy, a neighboring shop specializing in gummies, chocolates, and other sweets.

But its newest launch means you don't have to live anywhere near New York to get a taste of at least one of its viral treats.

The new Signature Hot Chocolate Mix costs $19.99 and comes with six individual sachets, each containing the same hot chocolate recipe served at Glace's shops.

According to the brand, the mix is made with ground chocolate and A2 milk powder, without the cornstarch or powdered fillers commonly used in conventional hot chocolate mixes. The result is designed to deliver the same rich, glossy consistency that made the drink famous.

Preparing it is pretty straightforward: Simply whisk the mix over medium-low heat on the stovetop until it transforms into a thick, decadent drinking chocolate. Sadly, the at-home version doesn’t come with the shop’s signature marshmallow rim...at least, not yet.

Glace says it's planning to release its signature marshmallow fluff separately, allowing customers to eventually recreate the full experience at home, toasted marshmallow rim and all. The brand hasn't announced an official release date for the fluff, but we're keeping an eye out.

For now, the hot chocolate mix is available for pre-order on Glace's website, with shipments expected to begin in early December.
